text: All the households of the village are expected to confine to the plots allocated to them in each year within the area assigned for that particular year. If anybody acts against this rule, the whole village suffers, because, if plots are cleared outside the area earmarked for a particular year, then the shifting cycle cannot be maintained and thus the fertility regained in the fallow periods cannot be enjoyed evenly by all the households. There is another reason why the households are expected to confine to the area earmarked for a particular year. At the time of setting fire, if the plots are in a compact block, villagers can fix a day when all can jointly control the fire. But if the plots are scattered, all the villagers run the risk of fire at the time of firing each plot. In Matchakolgiri during the three years of my investigation, I found a few households clearing jamang plots in the vicinity of the village. But these very little affected the shifting cycle of the village, as these were in the village precincts and were not in proper a’ba area. Moreover, during firing adequate precautions were taken so that fire could not spread to the village. So, there was no ground for objection by other villagers. In Wajadagiri nobody clears any jamang plot and all the shifting plots are cleared within the area earmarked for that particular year. This strong cooperation in mantaining the shifting cycle of the village marks off Ambengs from other subtribes of the Garo. In Chisak area, for example, households do not clear plots in a compact block ( vide p. 54).

To carry on such affairs successfully requires great patience and the ability to put up with repeated frustration. It is difficult for a man so much as to speak with a married woman without arousing immediate suspicion, with the result that the woman will then be closely watched by her husband’s relatives, increasing the difficulty of consummating an affair. The matrilocal extended family, with its women doing most of their work as a group; makes it difficult for a man to find his sweetheart alone. The lack of privacy in the small communities, where everyone knows what everyone else is doing, adds to this difficulty. The young man must be constantly on the alert so as not to miss the rare opportunities which come his way to arrange a rendezvous. For these reasons go-betweens are almost indispensable. text: I have now endeavoured to prove that, originally at any rate, impartial justice was not so difficult of attainment as investigations made FIG. 107. Yao Kramo, Tekiman Hene FIG. 108. Ohem[unavailable], Tekiman into the workings of Native tribunals at a later date might lead us to believe. Researches into the workings of early Ashanti law as opposed to its more modern application have revealed another interesting point. In olden days, before the rise of a powerful class of aristocracy, the chief aim of such central authority as existed seemed to have been the avoidance of possible causes of dispute and the conciliation of the parties temporarily estranged by litigation. In more modern times an exactly opposite result would appear to have become the goal of a central authority, which found itself powerful enough to quell serious disputes, if necessarily by force, and came to rely on the proceeds of litigation as a fruitful means of replenishing a depleted treasury. Litigation, in this somewhat degenerate epoch, came actually to be encouraged. Having given a decision, the courts were indifferent whether conciliation between the parties took place or not. A system of money payments in lieu of the death penalty further encouraged injustice and extortion. Councillors, instead of regarding a dearth of lawsuits as a blessing, came to look upon empty courts as a misfortune. Prayers were offered to the gods to send cases, and a Chief in whose time court fees dropped to a minimum was likely to be regarded not wholly with favour.

text: Then the two of them went dancing off, around the camp once and into the forest. There were a few last defiant bellows from the direction of the river, and no more was heard. The men stopped singing and prepared to eat. Two caldrons had been boiling over the fire, and both were now ready. One contained rice, the other a kind of spinach made from the leaves of the manioc plant. Eaten together they are delicious. I wondered if there would be any precedence as to who should eat first, or if there would be any ritual, but there was neither. Everyone ate his fill as and when he pleased, a couple of the older men saying they would wait until the youngsters had finished before they ate. But they did not wait for long. I was told, however, that everyone bad to eat, just as no adult male was allowed to sleep but bad to sing while molimo singing was in progress. Apparently one of the greatest crimes that a Pygmy male can commit, if not the greatest, is to be found asleep when the molimo is singing. One of the men stood up, and miming as all Pygmies love to do, he showed how they used to search for sleeping men, a spear under each arm, and how if they found one they would spear him in the stomach and kill him completely and for ever. I was told that then his body would be buried under the kumamolimo and nobody would be allowed to mention his death, even to remark on his absence. text: Now this attitude goes so deeply that it penetrates to the illegitimate appropriation of food. The natives distinguish between vayla'u , the stealing of food, and kwapatu , the stealing of any other object, and the first is infinitely more reprehensible and shameful. There are no arrangements for protecting the ripe crops in an open garden; during harvest, when everybody is busy taking out tubers and arranging them in heaps in the arbour, there are no arrangements for sleeping in the gardens or watching. I was often told that no one would ever vayla'u (steal produce). Still the very existence of the word and the very strong contempt felt by the natives at the idea of it suggests that cases must occur; but they are rare. The dangers of exposure and the shame of it are apparently a sufficiently strong protection against possible trespass. Moreover no one is in actual need of crops as food; for everybody when in need can automatically get enough from his kinsmen or relatives. In addition, to steal enough tubers to be worth taking into one's own arbour would be too difficult technically and too easily discovered. The sense of personal honour and ambition connected with good gardening is strongly developed. There is a moral attitude which would make an average Trobriander scorn the very idea of using somebody else's taytu. And it is this moral sentiment in conjunction with the actual arrangements, especially the publicity and openness of harvesting and the immediate stacking and display of taytu, which act as effective safeguards. 1 As far as I know, the Trobrianders have no belief in the stealing of tubers by magic--a belief which, according to Dr. R. text: The only individual who might be recognized as occupying a special political position in the life of the hunting band, on any ground other than age, is the camp clown. He is usually a hunter, and his position is unofficial, depending on his abilities as an actor and a clown. He is not appointed, and there is no special name for him or his position. However, every band seems to have its clown. His function is to act as a buff between disputants, deflecting the more serious disputes away from their original sources, absolving other individuals of blame by accepting it himself. Frequently he will end a dispute simply through the use of ridicule, and although such ridicule may be taken as a form of judgment, the essential point is that once again its objective is to divert attention from the source of the dispute and also to divert blame from anyone who is clearly in the wrong. The major concern of all, except possibly the prime disputants, is that the dispute shall be ended, and frequently by creating or reviving another, lesser dispute the clown brings the disputants into the same frame of mind. Everyone recognizes that the slightest rift in the band can lead directly to hunger through failure in economic co-operation.

text: According to the Annual Reports, the Korean nationalists cooperated with the socialists for the common cause of political emancipation and “availed themselves of every opportunity to arouse a national spirit among Koreans.” 106 Annual Report, 1934-35, p. 177. In 1924 a General Union of Chosen Workers and Farmers was organized, but its meetings were immediately forbidden, and “the new organs existed only in name.” But these organizations, though “existing only in name,” started building units throughout Korea. Soon after, the Korean Communist Party and the Korean Communist Young Men’s Association made their appearance. 107 It is important to note that communism and other “dangerous thoughts” came to Korea from Japan. “What greatly concerns me are the Korean students and laborers crossing to Japan proper who are apt to introduce various radical thoughts into Chosen after being infected in Japan Proper.” (from a speech of Governor-General Ugaki, made in 1933). In November 1925, “the greater part of their associates” were arrested at Shingishu. Others succeeded them and restored the organization but were also arrested in June 1926, together with conspirators who sought to use the state funeral of Prince Yi Wang for a demonstration. New members, braving prosecution, arrest, torture and execution, again restored the organization but were arrested in Keijo in 1929. At the same time, according to the Annual Reports, wholesale arrests of communists were made in Shingishu and Heijo. But the members of the Communist Party, “in spite of repeated arrests,” continued their propaganda and organizational work. We know from the authorities that during these years the nationalist, socialist, and communist movements “led the thoughts of young men into more dangerous ways, and many disgraceful occurrences took place,” but we are left in the dark as to the nature of these disgraceful occurrences.

text: The Eila represents the next level of tribal segmentation among the Awlad Ali. The Eila is the most important political unit. Although the Eila lacks any formally recognized leadership, its importance stems from the fact that it constitutes the vengeance group or Amar El-Dam (unity of the blood). This means that it bears a corporate responsibility for the actions of its members. Anyone of its members can be killed in vengence for a homocide committed by any other, and the duty of revenge for any member falls on all members alike, regardless of the exact genealogical relationship to the victim. When bloodmoney is to be paid, its members pay it as a group, divided among all male adults; and although when they receive it, a bigger portion goes to the nearest agnates of the victim, the remainder is distributed equally among all its members.

The dia or blood compensation money for physical injury, manslaughter, or murder is paid jointly by a man and his bu . Major, indeed most, meaningful inheritance such as land, household, liquid capital, and prerogatives to public office comes from a person’s agnatic kin, although some movable goods can be obtained through matrifilial connections; the same is true of bridewealth. They now seldom secure more than thirty beef tongues. An occurrence at another Sun-dance, during the ceremony of preparing the tongues, illustrates the methods employed by medicine men to impress upon the people their supernatural powers and the importance of implicit compliance with their directions. An Indian from Canada named Big Swan, with his wife, Good Hunter, were giving the Sun-dance. Big Swan selected as his adviser for the ceremonies, Spotted Eagle, and invited, to assist him, Red Wing, Wolf Eagle and Big Moon, with their wives Strikes-on-top, Feather Woman and Calls Back. They camped together on Two Medicine River, and were preparing the tongues. Big Swan interrupted the services by going to Willow Creek. There he met Spotted Eagle, telling him that additional tongues had been secured and the ceremonial would be continued that evening. For a moment Spotted Eagle made no reply, but gazed intently at the distant Rocky Mountains where his trained powers of observation detected signs of a storm. He said to Big Swan: “When you return to your tipi, do nothing further with the tongues to-night, put them away.” No more was said. Big Swan returned to Two Medicine River and told the waiting men and women of Spotted Eagle’s warning. Thinking they had insufficient reason for delay, they continued the service. In the midst of the ceremonial, a violent storm from the Rockies moved eastwardly over their camp. A bolt of lightning struck the lodge, prostrating the three women, Good Hunter, Strikes-on-top and Feather Woman. The last two recovered, but Good Hunter, the sacred woman, was killed. Big Swan discontinued the service, and, after placing the body of his wife upon a high cliff, overlooking the river, returned to Canada. In telling me of the event Spotted Eagle said: “It cast a deep gloom over the entire Sun-dance. If Big Swan had followed my directions it would not have happened. I saw signs of a storm over the mountains at the head of Two Medicine Canyon. title: The world of talk on a Fijian island: an ethnography of law and communication causation
text: Like all control communication institutions, the kinship centered system of conflict talk on Yanuyanu imposes its influence on structural communication in two ways: by providing a set of categories that define or redefine the substance of the conflict issue, and by enforcing a pattern of interaction through its procedural rules that govern the way participants in the conflict can communicate with one another. For example, the ritual apology, i soro , which is an integral part of the kinship control system, prescribes a set of roles that the participants must take, and those roles dramatically enact a powerfully hierarchical relationship pattern. As I have argued, hierarchy is instantiated in one-way communication in which one party is restrained and the other is free (see Figure 4.2). In the i soro , the penitent remains silent while the yaqona or whale's tooth he or she has brought is presented by a spokesman. The person offering the apology also looks down, cutting off visual communication, and must be dressed in a conservative, nonassertive way. Meanwhile the person to whom the apology is directed may respond directly--sometimes even sending the other person away angrily, although eventually the apology must be accepted.

title: Ideal norms and social control in Tarahumara society
text: 1. For a special sanctioning agent to be effective in enforcing his rulings, his position must be respected, and this respect may require force to back his decrees. Successful defiance of the gobernador cannot be permitted to escape punishment or this official’s prestige will wane. Rodrigo refused to help repair the school. The gobernador had announced that certain able-bodied men were required to lend this service. Rodrigo laughed at the gobernador and called him ‘worthless,’ a grave insult. The gobernador ordered the capitan to seize him and put him in jail. At a trial, Rodrigo was severly berated before the people, then fined six pesos. During the trial he remained silent and serious, because he was greatly humiliated. (Choguita.) In another trial a man received an especially heavy sentence for his reported defiance of the authority of the gobernador. A woman whose husband died, complained that an uncle had taken ten goats from the deceased’s herd which she felt belonged to her. She threatened to inform the gobernador of this, but he laughed and boasted that the gobernador could not do anything to him. When the trial was held, not only were the goats taken from the accused, but he was fined three pesos and held up as an example to others, that they do not also speak out against the native officials. (Norogachic.) 2. The native official himself must take his duties and obligations seriously. Where there is a weak gobernador and the lesser officials, mayor, and capitan, do not carry out their duties with energy, the people begin to slacken in bringing their disputes to these officials to be settled. The Sunday reunions are poorly attended, the pueblo religious festivals are badly planned and a bad performance results because of lack of cooperation from the dancers and musicians. The position of the capitan is of great importance because this official is the one who implements the decisions of the gobernador. He brings the accused to the pueblo to stand trial. He also acts as general liason officer by sending out his soldados (policemen and messengers) to inform all the people in outlying rancherias of the important Sunday reunions and ceremonial observances. Navaris was a capitan, and as a native official he was obliged to attend all Sunday reunions. Sunday after Sunday he missed these reunions. The gobernador ordered the soldados to bring Navaris to trial. He received a harsh semon reminding him of his duties. To better impress Navaris of the extent of his failings, he was made to spend a night in jail. (Choguita.) 3. The gobernador is impartial. In order for him to be able to judge impartially the merits of a case, the accuser must confront the accused with supporting evidence for the complaints made. It is for this reason that witnesses are always called upon during the trials. No one can be tried unless formally accused by someone who brings a complaint. Jesus Dias was accused of theft. The gobernador sent the capitan to bring Jesus to the Sunday reunion to be tried. On that Sunday, the accuser failed to appear to press charges. Despite the fact that Jesus had a bad reputation, the gobernador released him without a trial. (Norogachic.) 4. Extenuating circumstances are considered by the gobernador when making a judgment. Rodrigo, a child of about fourteen years, was accused of stealing beans from Benito’s storage bin. This child is an orphan whose parents died recently (early 1951) and he remained alone in the house, living on the food that remained in his parent’s stores. He fell into debt with a Mestizo, and in order to repay this debt, stole the beans. The gobernador was stern in his warnings to the child never to repeat such behavior, but he did not exact the severe punishment of whipping. The gobernador explained the lightness of the sentence on the grounds that the child was an orphan who had committed this theft under special circumstances, and that the child was not known to be a thief by reputation. (Norogachic.) Jose Maria began fighting with the gobernador secundo (the gobernador’s second in command) during a tesguinada. The capitan immediately threw Jose into jail to await trial. During the trial, no one could remember the reason for the brawl, so it was not possible to establish whether there was any serious provocation or not. Since Jose and the gobernador secundo were both drunk, the two were warned in a sermon to remember always to drink together peacefully. The gobernador explained after the trial that drunk people often lose their heads, and are therefore not really responsible for their actions. (Norogachic.) 5. The gobernador as head of a pueblo stands in an excellent position to control the behavior of individuals living in a geographically dispersed settlement pattern. Because he is a supra-rancheria figure, he is in a better position than the individual alone to recoup losses through theft. Unless the thief leaves the pueblo entirely, he cannot escape from the soldados of the gobernador. Mariquita was unable to find a cow. A neighbor, Lorenzo, informed her that Juan Chico now had her cow, and would probably attempt to take it to a rancheria in another pueblo. Mariquita notified the gobernador who sent his capitan after Juan. Juan had actually reached the outskirts of the next pueblo when he was overtaken. (Norogachic.) 6. Judgments are not slanted in favor of either men or women. There is equality of status. Josefa (woman) complained that Cantino’s oxen had ruined her corn field. Cantino brought the countercharge that Josefa’s animals and also ruined his crop. Witnesses were called who attested to the truth of both charge and counter-charge. The gobernador scolded both of them for failing to corral their animals during the planting time, an obligation demanded of all owners of animals. (Norogachic.) 7. All those who partake of stolen goods are liable to punishment. Martin and two other children stole a pig. Abran, a neighbor of the pig’s owner, who was visiting with Martin’s parents, noticed a pig skin whose color resembled that of a lost pig of his friend. Abran notified his friend, who brought charges against the entire family. The gobernador berated the parents for not advising the owner of the animal of the theft and for eating the meat and keeping the skin. They had to repay the owner for his loss with an ox. (Tatawichi.)

title: Tiv economy
text: BOTH SETS OF RIGHTS—to specific farms and to sufficient land—have easily recognized sanctions. Rights to specific farms are protected by ritual sanctions. Tiv erect magical emblems called akombo to protect farms against interlopers, thieves, and witches. This emblem consists of a bundle of sticks or a braided palm frond, a stone or a potsherd, placed on the ground or hung on a pole at the “top” of a field. The akombo are said to inflict disease or misfortune on anyone who meddles with the farm. The right to erect this magical emblem on a specific field is part of the basic cluster of rights in the field: a woman can erect an akombo on her own field; and her husband or the compound head can erect an akombo on this field. A woman may ask her husband to erect one on her farm, though more often he simply does it. A man can ask his compound head to erect an akombo on his farm; the compound head would not do so without being asked. No one else dares do so (unless he is paid by one of these three) lest the akombo attack the person who put it up.

text: One could argue that these taboos and fasting customs are simply cultural phenomena, traits inherited from earlier traditions and retained through inertia, and that no psychological processes need be invoked in describing them. But this argument fails to explain why, in view of the harmful physical and political consequences of their excessive fasting, the Amhara should have developed in the direction of increasing rather than alleviating their fasting burden. For Abyssinia’s commitment to fasting was well known by her enemies, and used to her disadvantage: Ahmad Gran took advantage of the country’s weakness during Lent to launch his attacks at that time year after year, and the Galla hordes who succeeded him did likewise. The argument also fails to explain why the taboos on pork and tobacco, and the fasting prescriptions, should have been pushed to the forefront of Amhara Christian consciousness. For observance of these mores is considered the very crux of Christianity by traditional Amhara. Amhara often refer to fasting as the most important part of their religion. If a person fails to fast, his relatives are technically absolved from the duty of providing memorial feasts for him when he dies; let his soul wander in darkness! Fasting more than anything else protects them from the devil and enhances the likelihood of their entering paradise.

text: The Ntam is used not only as a writ of summons but also to appeal to a higher court. To appeal to a higher court, one has to swear the Ntam of the particular chief to whose court the matter is being sent. It is the traditional form of the Roman formula ‘I appeal unto Caesar’. 49 49 St.Paul in Act of Apostles. 25:11 King James Version, Ohio. The chief whose immediate subjects the disputants are, then has certain duties: He has to slaughter a purification sheep and send the thigh to his overlord. This is to inform him of the violation of his Ntam. The chief would then set a date to re-hear the case, examining the witnesses and taking fresh evidence. This is to be contrasted with the practice of appellate tribunals in the common law system. The appellate tribunals, normally, neither see the parties nor take fresh evidence but merely examine the evidence taken by the court of first instance. The traditional court however does the opposite. This is not strange considering that no written records of the proceedings are kept by the court of first instance.

text: Out of sympathy for the two women the other men did not wish to tolerate this situation any longer. Everyone felt as unwise any open, obvious offense or surreptitious murder -- both possibilities had been considered in strict secrecy. The Argentine police would certainly have intervened if Nana had been seriously wounded or murdered. In this harsh mood of all the men against Nana, the long widowed Hotex reached a decision in April, 1923, to take Juana. He first discussed it with Toin, and when the latter assured him of the help of the influential Tenenesk, a few other men were easily won over. One day, when most of the men were out hunting, Hotex took advantage of the opportunity and in secret discussion obtained the consent of old Catalina; the latter, for her part, promised to win her daughter over to the plan of a flight and marriage with Hotex. 347 After a few days Hotex and Juana met in an inconspicuous spot; she begged him to free her from this desperate situation, she would gladly run away with him as his wife. They intended to wait until spring; then Hotex, on a suitable day, would suddenly hasten far into the north of Isla Grande with Juana and take a job with a farmer; Catalina, however, would meanwhile have to find shelter with another family, if Nana, as was to be feared, began to vent his wrath on her. This, in turn, was to be the summons to the other men first to release diatribes against 347 cont. Nana and to provoke him to action. The plan was to work on him with sticks so that he would be incapable of resistance for several months; during this time the runaway couple could live together in all peace. For the future the men promised sharp vigilance over Nana in order to make any reaction impossible for him. If he saw himself completely alone against solid opposition, he would not dare to make serious attempts to harm his rival and Juana, who had fled with him. Later on old Catalina would possibly visit the hut of her new son-in-law ... But already toward the end of the same winter Juana died. This incident seems a good example of the unwritten marriage law of our Selk'nam, which, under certain circumstances, even permits the abduction of a married person.

title: Ideal norms and social control in Tarahumara society
text: The existence of numerous cases of conflict between individuals does not mean that Tarahumara society as presently constituted cannot continue to maintain itself and is in a state of disintegration. If agencies exist that succeed in restoring harmony between contending parties, then even frequent complaints and disputes are not signs of progressive deterioration of the society. The real sign of deterioration is a condition in which all informal and formal pressures no longer can control such behavior. Temporary states of conflict may be frequent and still not threaten a general collapse of interpersonal relations or signify a complete failure of ideal norms to influence behavior. As long as the Tarahumaras are willing to let the native officials settle the disputes that cannot be resolved by informal methods, and will respect the judgments made, then potentially, at least, all conflict situations can be resolved. There is a definite distinction that must be drawn between conflicts which are frequent but resolvable, and conflicts which the society can no longer effectively handle. In Tarahumara society, verbalized complaints are in themselves a mechanism whereby bad interpersonal relations become externalized and discussed. The Tarahumara do not suppress their hostilities to the extent that such tribes as the Zuni do, so it would be unfair in comparing tribes to use overt signs of conflict alone as a criterion for social strife.

text: Tlingit warfare followed the general pattern of that of the other tribes of the area. But, as is true of much of the primitive world, it is impossible to draw the line between petty feuds at one end of the scale and open hostility between much larger groups at the other end. It is most important to note that feuds and wars were seldom betweent ribe and tribe as such or even between village and village. I learned of only two such feuds. One was between the Tantakwan and the Kitkatlah tribe of the Tsimshian. Otherwise they were always between clan and clan, though the trouble might spread and involve other clans. In native theory most feuds which expanded into war were between clans of the opposite moieties, but from the accounts given me it seems certain that intramoiety hostilities were also fairly common.

The roofed gallery, the ruai , is probably the most interesting part of the longhouse, however, as most tasks and interactions take place here, from food-preparation, gossiping, news-exchange and story-telling to mourning rituals, invocations and other sacred rites. Here also the tuai rumah , or village head-man, mediates between disputing parties so that the ritual balance of the whole longhouse community will not be endangered, and discussions are carried on about ventures and ideas that are of joint interest to all bilek -families. 18 A.J.N. Richards, personal communication. A.J.N. Richards, personal communication. The young, un-married men sleep here and up close to the ceiling hang the highly treasured antu pala , the smoke-dried, blackened heads taken from former enemies. Like most other possessions in Iban society these are owned by the bilek -family and are not the common property of the whole community. In fact there is only one part of the longhouse that is jointly owned and that is the notched ladder (-s) that lead up to the open tanju platform. The latter is mainly used as a drying place for a variety of things, the most noteworthy being padi , which ultimately gets stored in bark-tubs in the sadau . The whole house structure is placed on supporting posts to avoid the risk of flooding, to make the house safer from animals and, in former times, to make it easier to defend. The house should never be built across a stream nor should it be directly facing another across the river. The reason for the latter I do not know, but the former probably comes from streams being used as boundary marks between adjacent communities plus the fact that household refuse gets dropped through slits in the floor onto the ground under the house to feed the domestic pigs, which occupy this area.

text: For exacting truth, torture is customary, t[unknown] ena en obíni , i.e., tie the string! The string of a bow is tied so tightly around the upper arm of the defendant that it cuts into the flesh. If the testimony has not succeeded in convicting the defendant and if he cannot prove his innocence by an alibi, an ordeal is used. The most common is the ol momai l os sarge , i.e., the ordeal of the blood. The defendant is given a bowl with a mixture of blood and milk. Before he drinks, he says the words: 'Ng ai a-ok elle sarge, t[unknown] ena nanu ajawa ena gete[unknown] n, na[unknown] ea elle sarge , i.e., God, I drink this blood, if I have taken that head of cattle this blood will kill me. If the defendant does not die after eight to fourteen days, proof of his innocence is provided by that. Another ordeal is the ol momai l en jerta natoijo , i.e., the ordeal of the dry wood. By accepting these, he invites God's punishment upon himself if he is guilty. He will then soon 220 be dead like the dry branch, whereas otherwise he will remain vigorous and healthy, as the green one still is. Less common is the 220 cont. ol momai l e[unknown] n gauo , the ordeal of the bow. A bow is placed on the ground and a magic horn is set at either end of it. This is a goat horn that is filled with a medicine made by a sorcerer. As soon as the defendant has stepped over the bow, his lot will be, if he is guilty, the punishment of God, that is, in this case death. The effect of the ordeals rests on the firm belief in them. The guilty one is convinced that the punishment of God will have to strike him. He imagines that he is ill and sees his salvation only in an open confession. He goes to the one robbed, confesses his deed, pays the customary fine, and begs for forgiveness. Only by gaining the latter can he escape the consequences of the false oath. The one robbed must in this case -- if he himself does not wish to invite the punishment of God on himself -- grant the pardon and does so through words and spittings, whereby at the same time a friendship is initiated between the two. Besides the aforementioned ordeals there are two others which are not accompanied by curses. The ol momai l ol origa l en gulugok or ol momai 1 ol origa 1 e[unknown] n gob - the ordeal of the stool made of earth. The defendant must sit down on a specially prepared lump of earth. If this crumbles under him, he is regarded as guilty. The other one, the ol momai 1 e[unknown] n gine (of the goat), is used only if the defendant is a non-Masai. The defendant, standing, takes a goat between his legs and cuts an ear off it. If the blood issuing from the cut spatters him, he is guilty.

text: As among the Masai, the legal view makes no distinction between murder and manslaughter, but indeed between the latter and negligent homicide. A murderer caught in the very act is subject to blood revenge, for the execution of which every man belonging to the family of the one murdered and in some districts also any of his friends and campmates are justified. If the avengers do not succeed in capturing the murderer on the day of the murder, 262 the latter is safe from blood revenge, for people see in the unsuccessful search for him a command of God to let him live. To atone for his deed, however, he must pay the principal heir of the deceased one large and two small ivory tusks. Negligent homicide is punished by the payment of a medium-sized ivory tusk. If the perpetrator and the one who was killed belong to the same lineage, the punishment is considerably less than if they are from different lineages of the same tribe. On the other hand, if the two belong to different tribes, the ones entitled to blood revenge often hand over the execution of it to the Masai, who kill the perpetrator, even if they do not capture him until after several months. Up to the completed payment the perpetrator is regarded as puni-and[unknown] et , corresponding to the ol oikobani of the Masai. If an Asá kills a Masai blacksmith, the deed remains unpunished because the blacksmiths are too weak for revenge and the Masai would 262 cont. never have anything to do with taking their part. On the other hand, if an Asá is killed by a blacksmith, the Masai immediately place themselves on the side of the ones injured and avenge murder, manslaughter, or negligent homicide by murdering the perpetrator. The Wandor[unknown] obo, to be sure, would themselves be in a position to execute the revenge, but the Masai do not permit this because they see in it an encroachment on their rights as masters of the land and in particular also of the el konono.

text: The descendants of Ijaaj-Enona, who reside in the village of Botukebo, have distinguished themselves in several respects. First, they are known as fierce and courageous warriors who often fought victoriously in battles in which they were greatly outnumbered. They were also widely known because their leaders often conducted very turbulent politics. In the political field the village is represented nowadays by the sublineage leader Ijaaj Awiitigaaj, a wealthy headman ( tonowi ) whose fortune consisted (in September 1955) of two houses; four pigs; cash of 60 Km (old native cowrie shells), 120 Tm (new cowrie shells introduced by the white man), and 300 b (large blue glass beads); credits of 1,500 Km and 420 b ; 20 machetes; and 20 large bead necklaces. He is not regarded as too generous and is credited with a high temper, a characteristic which on several occasions has brought the villagers, and ultimately the confederacy, into unnecessary wars. His bravery in combat is seldom matched by other Kapauku; in battle he has been wounded 14 times; the resulting scars he displays with pride and affection. His powers nowadays are not contested by anyone, and most of the villagers follow his advice. Several times in the past his volatile temper has caused clashes with other parts of the same confederacy. At such times Awiitigaaj was the master mind behind organized stick fights which almost never settled a problem but always cooled off heads and presented Awiitigaaj with an opportunity to reassert himself as an excellent and dangerous foe. In the recent past the village of Botukebo also became well known because of its internal political problems. Although in 1954 Botukebo represented a solid political unit under the able leadership of Awiitigaaj, only two years earlier it was still torn by strife between the present leader and Dimiidakebo, another determined contestant for the leadership. The people of Botukebo formed two political factions, each led by one of the men. Although Dimiidakebo also was rich and brave, he could not match Awiitigaaj in shrewdness, eloquence, and number of wives. Although he challenged Awiitigaaj’s leadership in several fights, he never succeeded in unseating his opponent. This was primarily due to the fact that Dimiidakebo failed to comply with the basic moral requirement of Kapauku leadership; not only was he more selfish than Awiitigaaj, but he also delighted in committing frauds, borrowing money under false pretenses, and seldom returning in full what he borrowed. As a consequence, only 12 people followed him, all of whom were his close patrilineal relatives. Awiitigaaj mustered support from exactly twice as many men as his opponent managed to rally. Even impartial households were ultimately dragged into the conflict. They sent half of their males to one side and half to the other. As a consequence two identical twin sons of Timaaj, for example, found themselves fighting with sticks on opposite sides. (Of course, they did not fight each other, but picked their personal enemies who happened to be fighting for the opposite side and gave them a thorough beating. Thus the motives of many of the fighting force were often completely divorced from the official cause of trouble as proclaimed by the two leaders.) Finally Dimiidakebo began to lose the trust and esteem of most of the uncommitted people to the extent that the other headmen of the confederacy turned against him and decided on his execution. This outcome was to no small extent due to Awiitigaaj’s shrewd political machinations. In order to eliminate Dimiidakebo as painlessly as possible, all of the headmen resorted to black magic. According to my informants, throngs of evil spirits and departed shadows, the supernatural helpers of the headmen, attacked the bad man and finally succeeded in expelling his soul from his body. Dimiidakebo suddenly died in 1953, leaving the leadership of Botukebo to the victor, Awiitigaaj.

text: Until the 1900's, when the average Lozi commoner married he gave the bride's parents a few hoes and mats. It is comparatively recently (1900-10) that their paramount chief Lewanika issued a law that two beasts or [unknown]2 should be given for a virgin and one beast or [unknown]1 for a girl who is not a virgin (a widow, a divorcee, an unmarried girl who has had a child, or an unmarried woman who is so long past puberty she should not be a virgin). To constitute legal marriage now there must be consent of the parties and consent of the bride's parents or guardians, which is implicit in their accepting the marriage payment. The last is the most important indicator of a legal marriage, at which a Lozi court looks to see if it will award adultery damages if another man sleeps with the woman. If her parents have consented to the union but the man has not delivered the cattle or money, the court will not award him damages. It will say that she is his concubine, ‘a wife of the country’. Thus the marriage payment gives a man the right to exclude other men from his wife and the right to control her. Though divorce is frequent and a woman can get it easily, if her husband resists she must go to court. If she refuses point-blank to live with her husband, neither he nor the courts can compel her to do so. If she deserts him he can always in this polygynous society take other wives or concubines, while she can only lie with or go to another man under threat of an adultery charge, when her lover will pay damages of two cattle to the husband, or three if she has come to him as a wife, and she will have to pay a fine of one head to the court. (These fines were raised by [unknown]2 in 1947, after this essay was first written.) Thus ultimately a woman, if her lover is eager to have her, can force a divorce from her husband. When an abductor pays damages to the husband the latter loses his rights over his wife. If she agrees to return to her husband she remains his wife; but she can remain with her abductor. The third beast he gave to the husband counts as a marriage-beast. This usually happened in the past. To control these moves the Lozi have made it a criminal offence for a woman's abductor to give her parents the fine she must now pay the court.

Much of the land which the new immigrants occupied was apparently claimed by Milikin, as the Sadong District Officer mentioned their complaints in several of his reports ( Sarawak Gazette 815, 1 Nov. 1921, p. 160; 825, 1 June 1922, p. 152). In spite of the fact that in a 1921 report the Brooke officer in charge of the area remarked that the Milikin were excessively greedy in wishing to keep immigrant Iban out of large tracts of unused forest, in 1929 some Iban were fined heavily by the government for farming on the Ensebang River in Milikin territory ( Sarawak Gazette 916, 2 Jan. 1930, p. 24), and in 1936 all immigration of Iban from other Divisions into the Sadong basin was forbidden. By that time any exploitation of the upper Ensebang by Iban or any others was considered illegal, as the area had, in the previous year, been gazetted as the Balai Ringin Protected Forest ( Sarawak Government Gazette 28(26), 2 Dec. 1935, p. 726).

title: Social change in Tikopia
text: A special category of adultery by Christian standards was polygyny which was, of course, licit in traditional Tikopia custom. The priest stated to me in 1952 that he allowed a polygynist to return to the Church, but only after he had put away one of his wives. This was consistent with his disciplinary rules of a generation before, but appeared to be more rigorously enforced with the growth of the Christian body. A Christian who committed adultery to the extent of actually taking his paramour to live openly with him and his wife --though married by Tikopia custom--was hardened in sin. Of the three such cases in 1952 of Tikopia polygynists (cf. p. 205), two of the men and five of the women were Christians. An example was Kasoavae of the lineage of Vainunu. He was baptised by the name of Ellison--taking the priest's name--and later reverted to paganism. He married a daughter of Pa Nukutauo, and then six months later he married her elder sister also. Both sisters were called Nau Rangitaukena in accordance with the house name he had taken--not by different house names as would have been more usual. Both women who, too, had been baptised, lived in the one house with their husband. I talked with the women, who seemed very content. I asked ‘Is it good? One of them replied ‘Yes, it is good.’ Here their brother-in-law, who was present, added ‘It is not wrong. Look at my daughters in Fatumaru.’ (These were twins, also married polygynously.) This husband had deserted the Church before he married, so no sanction could be taken against him. But one of his sons, a boy of about three years, had been refused baptism by the priest. For a long time the women had not gone to Church but to the pagan rites in Uta. Recently, however, one of them had begun to go to Church again and had apparently been allowed to do so by the priest--probably not in recognition of the marriage but as a move in recalling all parties to an appreciation of their sin.

Failure to follow the word of any of these people brings social sanctions to bear on the individual, and in many cases these sanctions are severe enough to mean jail. It is also true that the sanctions will be applied with varying severity since they are frequently a family matter and a matter of common law, just as in our own society where there are severe and lenient parents or a favorite child may receive special favors and less punishment than a non-favorite. Finally, there is the ever-present economic pressure forcing performance of certain duties or hunger for oneself as well as for the members of one’s family. There are, without doubt, advantages in freedom from hard work for the man who is clever at winning loyalty and gifts from admiring friends and relatives. Among those Trukese who worked for the rulers, Japanese and American, it is and was something of a recognized game to get as much as possible from their employers in the way of the things the Trukese value, food and pisek . There are recognized ways of dealing with this situation among Trukese, but the unknowing foreigner is frequently extremely shocked by this behavior.

title: The Mayawyaw ritual: VI. illness and its ritual
text: The Mayawyaw, in order to protect against thieves the fruits on betel nut trees, pomelo trees and the like, or to prevent the stealing of sugar cane, often perform some rites (see infra ) at the foot of such trees or near such plants they own, on account of which the bu’djuy tumor is believed to have been made adhaerent, in a spiritual way, to that tree or these plants. A man who performs these rites (or invites a priest to perform them) will usually inform his neighbors: these will evidently not take the risk of getting a bu’djuy, but the others who know nothing about the performance of these rites might climb upon a tree and steal some fruits. Besides that, one could hardly find one Mayawyaw who would not steal a betel nut, some chewing-leaves, a sugar cane stalk or some other fruits, when he has such desires and a good opportunity. Such a custom, most common and in itself not considered as very bad by the Mayawyaw, makes that no one who got a bu’djuy will refuse to admit that he committed such a larceny: the bu’djuy itself is always considered the proof of the theft. It is also necessary that he admits his guilt, and even he must reveal from which tree he took the fruits or chewing-leaves or where he took the the sugar cane, for only the priest, who performed the rites at the foot of the tree or near the plants, can successfully perform the rites to cure the bu’djuy . Perhaps no rites at all were performed at that tree or near these plants in question! In this case they will not draw the conclusion that the bu’djuy is due to another cause, but they will say: “the rites have been performed probably by one or another ancestor of the actual owner”, or, “he has perhaps stolen some fruits from another tree but forgot it.” Anyway the bu’djuy rites will be done, but then by any priest who is initiated: if he is not successful, it will most probably be explained that he could not remove the bu’djuy for not being the very priest wanted.

One of these stories is so thrilling that I will endeavour to reproduce it in brief. A Kürdish lady was returning, accompanied only by a manservant, to her husband's house from a visit to her parents, who lived a day's journey off. On the road this man contrived so many delays that, instead of reaching home before sunset, they were obliged to stop for the night at a lonely and untenanted khan, of evil repute as the resort of robbers and brigands. After stabling the horses, the man came upstairs to the room occupied by his mistress, and approached her with dishonouring proposals. But she, divining his intention, had ready a small knife, which she plunged into his throat as he laid hold of her, and he fell dead. Not daring to close her eyes in that horrible place, she crouched in a corner to await the dawn. About midnight she was startled by hearing the sound of horse's hoofs approaching the khan--for who but a malefactor could arrive there in the dead of night? The newcomer alighted, and appeared to be seeking a stable for his horse, as he was leading it about below. “If he finds our horses,” she thought, “I am lost,” and again seizing the knife she cut off one of the dead man's arms and flung it from the window at the stranger as he passed below. He, however, still continued to wander backwards and forwards, leading his horse; so the next time he passed she cut off the other arm and threw that also at him. Upon this he cried, “Whosoever ye be, know that I am Dergo of Kisan, 1 A town between Bitlis and Van. and I fear ye not!” Oh, joy! It was her husband's voice.

Since no one can be expected to fulfil an obligation if its fulfilment entails disaster, the easiest way of eluding an undertaking is to say that the oracles have informed you that if you were to embark upon it you would die. No one can expect you to court disaster. Good faith is therefore sometimes abused. If you merely do not wish to send your son to act as a page at the king’s court, or to accompany your friend to Bongo country, or to give your daughter in marriage to the man to whom you have pledged her, or to allow your wife to visit her parents, you have only to plead that the oracles prophesy death as the outcome of these ventures. However, by these circumlocutions you may delay but not permanently avoid carrying out your obligations; for the persons to whom you are pledged, your king, your friend, your future son-in-law, your parents-in-law will also consult their oracles to check your oracles, and even if the declarations of their oracles agree with what you have untruthfully stated to be the declarations of your oracles they will only release you for a while from your obligations. Efforts will at once be made by those concerned to find the witch whose influence threatens your future, and when they have persuaded him to withdraw his influence you will have to think of a new excuse if you do not wish to carry out your obligations. Thus oracles, as explained more fully in the Part devoted to them, are used as a means of compelling behaviour, and their authority may also be used improperly to avoid duties. Nevertheless, no Zande would state the declaration of an oracle other than it was given. If he wishes to lie he fakes an oracular declaration without consulting the oracles at all.

title: Property, kin, and community on Truk
text: As noted above, the relations between a chief and the people of his district are patterned largely after the relations between the parties in divided ownership. As provisional title holders to territory, the various lineages owe the chief periodic gifts of produce from the land. These gifts are rendered at stated times in connection with feasts given in the chief’s honor. He fixes the time for these feasts in accordance with a seasonal calendar: two feasts during the breadfruit season, and two more during the turmeric season. 11 11 The Trukese divide the year into two main seasons, each of approximately six months’ duration: rääs , the breadfruit season, lasting roughly from July to December, and jefen the turmeric season, lasting from January to June. The men of the various lineages prepare breadfruit in giant wooden bowls while the women fish. Other types of food are also collected. On the day of the feast each lineage brings its food in a procession, the men carrying the giant bowls on frames and chanting as they walk. The food is carried into the meeting house of the chief’s lineage. The chief then selects the largest bowl for himself and his lineage mates and redistributes the rest of the food to the assembled population. The distribution is made according to lineage and is roughly proportional to the size of each lineage. The contributions which each lineage makes are also proportional to the size of its membership and the amount of productive land which it controls. If a lineage fails in this obligation, the chief has the right to confiscate its holdings. Should he indicate dissatisfaction with the contribution of a particular lineage, its members will hasten to prepare additional food and other gifts to mollify him.

title: Modern and traditional administration of justice in New Guinea
text: Traditional Kapauku sanctions . The Kapauku’s basic value of individual freedom and their conception of the essence of life (the free cooperation of body and soul), was clearly reflected in the way they punished offenders and redressed wrongs. People could not be forced into desired behavior: an offender could not be beaten into performing a task, a child could not be compelled to conform to its parents’ desires or requests; only inducement was possible. All sanctions were punishments for, or rectification of, past delicts and mistakes. In this way justice ( uta - uta ) was achieved by balancing, so to speak, the past suffering of the plaintiff with the present suffering of the defendant. Since a man’s freedom of action had to be kept unimpaired, a culprit could not be arrested and brought to face the authorities; he had to be induced to appear by threat of economic, social, or bodily harm. Similarly, there was no place in the Kapauku culture for slaves, serfs, prisoners of war, jail inmates, or hostages. The penal institution so prevalent in the West and in the rest of the civilized world of today, the jail, was not known. A preponderance of sanctions (about 90 percent of the cases) took economic and/or psychological form. Damages, restitutions, indemnities, and other material transfers and payments were exacted even for major crimes such as murder, rape, fornication, and assault. Not until a culprit refused to fulfill the obligation imposed by a sentence was he physically punished by beating, wounding with an arrow in his thigh, or executed. Only a murderer who became notorious for killing people did not have the option of compensation: he would be shot to death. But even capital punishment did not involve tying the sentenced man and forcing him to stand to be executed. No ritual ceremony was made of execution, as is the case in our civilization. Rather, it was done from ambush, when a firing squad, usually of four to eight members, shot their arrows from behind into the unsuspecting culprit (the death sentence was pronounced in secret, after the man had had a chance to defend himself and was found guilty). To eliminate any internal rift, the closest patrilineal relative of the sentenced man (son, father, brother, patriparallel cousin) was required to be a member of the firing squad. However, he was allowed, out of humane consideration, to miss the victim.

text: There are two types of restriction upon the use of economic resources which are not classified by the Tikopia as tapu . The first consists in a verbal prohibition such as a chief will utter against breaking up a certain area of land for taro planting. The sanction behind this prohibition 1 [against breaking up a cetain area of land for taro planting--Analyst] is respect for him, fear of his anger and perhaps of supernatural punishment by his gods, coupled with the recognition that such a prohibition is usually dictated by common sense as when the ground has not lain fallow long enough to yield the best crop. But in the absence of any specific ritual performance and of any material token of the prohibition, it rests outside the tapu classification. The second type of prohibition consists primarily in a material token, but has no ritual to bring it into the tapu sphere. If, for instance, a man wishes to reserve the fruit of a few coco-nut or areca palms, or a Canarium almond tree for his own use, he lashes some sago fronds to the trunk. This is a sign to all that they should leave such trees untouched. It applies perticularly to near relatives and friends who in the ordinary way might be expected to cull the fruit without first asking the owner's permission. This sign is called a pipi , being a form of the word pi , to block. It is really an indication that permission is withheld. It may be put up by any commoner or chief. The same aim is sometimes sought by laying branches across a path or by filling up the entrance in the hedge which surrounds an orchard.

title: The Lapps in Finland up to 1945. Vol. 2
text: Lapps from Norway and Sweden, on the other hand, also spent part of the winter or other seasons on the Finnish side. The mountain-Lapps of Tana, 11 families, who around 1744 spent their summers on the peninsula between the Tana-and Varanger-fiords (Varjagnjarga), migrated for the winter to the regions on both sides of the lake and river Pulmanki, “which area has always been considered Norwegian” (nowadays the major part of the lake and the whole river belong to Finland). The mountain-Lapps of Laksefiord (from the commune of Kjöllefiord), being more numerous, migrated rather to the Tana River area for the winter. When the lichen was exhausted, they crossed the river to the region of Jeskadam and Njullasjöhka, the latter an affluent of Kietsimä. Later on, when their number was reduced, they joined the Tana-Lapps and arrived for the winter at the regions of the lake and river Pulmanki. 2 HELLAND, m.t., pp. 121-24, 126-28, 136. Around 1850, the nomad-Lapps of eastern Norwegian Lapland, not including the inhabitants of southern Varanger, migrated between November and the end of the year along the river Neiden (Näytämö) as far as Iijärvi and Lake Inari. If there were no reindeer to tend, this migration started in August-October. Lapps called Tomma and Bigga, from eastern Norwegian Lapland, migrated to Utsjoki and Inari and even as far as Saariselkä. 1 PAULAHARJU, Taka-Lappia, p. 100. Borg[unknown] a T. 1840, n:o 8: The Norwegian Lapps put their own marks on Inari-fawns and damage the wild-reindeer traps of the Paadar-Lapps. The Karasjok-Lapps moved to northwestern Inari, and later mainly to the region of Jorgastak, near Utsjoki. Some of them went before Christmas, others after, but most of them went only for Candlemas (2 February). They tended their reindeer for two to three months on the Finnish side. The Kautokeino-Lapps, except for some families with only a few reindeer, arrived in the latter half of December and in January at Enontekiö and Muonio, and at Tepasto near Kittilä. The return began on the feast of the Annunciation. A small part of these Lapps returned to Karesuando for the winter via Enontekiö. Some Karesuando-Lapps spent the winter near the Norwegian-Finnish borders. They tended their herds now on the Norwegian, now on the Finnish side, according to circumstances, sometimes advancing many miles across the border. The migrations of the Norwegian and Swedish Lapps to Finland came to an end on the whole when the closing of the border by the Administration took effect (see chapter Reindeer-breeding, p.326). Even after the closing of the border, some of the Karesuando-Lapps (e.g. those from Kön-Kämä and Keinovuopio) migrated to Skibotn and Skarvdal via Finnish territory and across the large, open swamplands of Siilas, Poro and Romma. They still do so today. If the herds got mixed up on the way, they were separated on the Finnish side, where the ox herds often were left during calving time. Many Karesuando-Lapps who migrated in summer to Falsnes, on the coast, let their female reindeer calve at Enontekiö. The autumn- and winter-pastures of the above-mentioned Swedish Lapps had formerly been situated on the Finnish side. After the closing of the border, some of the Kautokeino-Lapps migrated in summer to Juovaggi via Porovuoma, returning the same way in autumn. During the spring migration the Lapps usually chose their course so as to avoid other herds and reach certain grazing grounds before the others. During the trip they also observed pasture possibilities, as well as weather and other natural conditions, e.g. overflowing rivers, etc. 1 Renbeteskomm. af 1913 handl. I:1, pp. 40, 72-5, 78, 88, 90, 104. Under normal conditions the migrations turned out well or fairly well. In spring they usually advanced at night when there was a hard crust on the snow, but if the snow was hard throughout, the hungry reindeer tried to get to the mountains day and night, in which case the people hardly had time to eat, let alone to rest. When the Lapps set off for Norway after calving, they were often caught in severe snowstorms, or in rain or sleety rain, in which case the travelers got soaked through. The migrations were also interrupted by open rivers, across which the men had to wade carrying the other family members. During the return in autumn the weather might be rainy in the mountains, making the trip and life in the hut particularty trying. In early winter the conditions were at times so bad that it was impossible to advance either on foot or driving; the draft-reindeer might get so tired that the men had to pull the sleds. Those who suffered most on these migrations were the old, the sick, and particularly the small children, as it was impossible to feed them regularly or give them dry clothes.

text: This proclamation is called khang shnong , and by it all are stopped from going anywhere from the village the following day. Anybody who disregards the prohibition is liable to fine. The following day, towards evening, all the grown-up males of the village assemble at the durbar ground, the site of which is marked in some villages by rows of flat stones, arranged in an irregular circle, upon which the durbaris sit. The proceedings are opened by one of the headmen, who makes a long speech; then others follow, touching upon all sorts of irrelevant matters, but throwing out hints, now and then, bearing on the subject of accusation. By degrees the debate waxes warmer, and the parties get nearer the point. Then the complainant and the defendant each of them throw down on the ground a turban, or a bag containing betul and pán , lime, &c. , in front of the durbar. These are regarded as the pledges of the respective parties and their representatives in the suit; they receive the name of mamla (hence the Khasi term ar liang mamla for the two contending parties in the suit). There are pleaders on both sides called 'riw said , who address the durbar in lengthy speeches, the Siem being the judge and the whole body of the durbar the jury. Witnesses are examined by the parties; in former times they were sworn on a pinch of salt placed on a sword. The most sacred and most binding form of oath, however, is sworn on u klong (a hollow gourd containing liquor). As, however, the latter form of oath is regarded by the Khasis as a most serious ordeal, it will be described separately. The durbar sometimes goes on for several days. At length the finding of the durbar is taken, after the Siem has summed up, and sentence is pronounced, which generally consists of a fine in money, almost always accompanied by an order to the losing party to present a pig. The pig is supposed to be sacrificed to a goddess, Ka 'lei synshar , i.e. the goddess of the State, but it is invariably eaten by the Siem and the members of the durbar. The Siem then calls out “ kumta mo khynraw ” (is it not so, young people?) The members of the durbar then reply, “ haoid kumta khein khynraw ” (yea, it is so, young ones). Sentences of fine are more often resorted to than other punishments nowadays, probably because very few of the Siems possess jails for the reception of criminals. The condemned one in a criminal case frequently serves his time by working for the Siem as a menial servant. The above descrip tion, which is based on the account given by the Rev. W. Lewis, with some modifications, may be taken as the usual form of procedure of the Khasi durbar.

title: The Khasis
text: The Khasi saying is, “ long jaid na ka kynthei ” (from the woman sprang the clan). The Khasis, when reckoning descent, count from the mother only; they speak of a family of brothers and sisters, who are the great grandchildren of one great grandmother, as shi kpoh , which, being literally translated, is one womb, i.e. the issue of one womb. The man is nobody. If he is a brother, u kur , a brother being taken to mean an uterine brother, or a cousin-german, he will be lost to the family or clan directly he marries. If he be a husband, he is looked upon merely as u shong kha , a begetter. In some of the Wár villages a newly married man is spoken of by the bride's family as, “ u khun ki briew ,” some one else's son. It is, perhaps, somewhat of a paradox under the circumstances that wives should address their husbands as “ kynrad ,” or lord. There is, however, no gainsaying the fact that the husband, at least in theory, is a stranger in his wife's home, and it is certain that he can take no part in the rites and ceremonies of his wife's family, and that his ashes after death can find no place within the wife's family tomb, except, in certain cases, amongst the Syntengs. Further, the ceremonial religion amongst Khasis, espceially that of the home, is in the hands of the women. It is, therefore, perhaps not to be wondered at, considering the important status assigned to women by the Khasis, that women should inherit the property and not men. The rule amongst the Khasis is that the youngest daughter “holds” the religion, “ ka bat ka niam .” Her house is called, “ ka iing seng ,” and it is here that the members of the family assemble to witness her performance of the family ceremonies. Here is, therefore, the largest share of the family property, because it is she whose duty it is to perform the family ceremonies, and propitiate the family ancestors. The other daughters, however, on their mother's death are entitled, each of them, to a share of their mother's property, although the youngest daughter gets the lion's share, e.g. the family jewellery, and the family house, and the greater part of what it contains. The youngest daughter cannot dispose of the house without the unanimous consent of her sisters. If the youngest daughter dies, she is succeeded by the next youngest daughter, and so on. All the daughters are bound to repair the house of the youngest daughter free of cost. In the event of the youngest daughter changing her religion, or committing an act of sang , or taboo, she loses her position in the family, and is succeeded by her next youngest sister, as in the case of a death. Failing daughters, inheritance would pass by the “knight's move” to the sister's youngest daughter, who would be succeeded by her youngest daughter, and so on. Failing sister's daughters succession would revert to the mother's sisters and their female descendants. In the Jaintia Hills the inheritance of all real property passes from mother to youngest daughter. No man in the uplands of the Jaintia Hills can possess landed property, unless it is self-acquired property. In the Jaintia Hills, if a man dies and leaves acquired property, his heir will be his mother, if alive, excluding wife, sons, and daughters. If the wife, however, undertakes not to re-marry, she will inherit half of her husband's property, which at her death will descend to her youngest daughter by him.

text: It can be seen from this that the Iban family is clearly a significant right-bearing unit in a jural sense. In addition to rights in tangible property, the family is also the focus of a complex of social rights and duties traditionally enjoined and upheld by adat . Some elements of family law are discussed here, particularly in connection with marriage, divorce and adoption, but a more detailed description of the jural nature of the family, provisions of member-ship, inheritance and division of its properties can be found in Freeman (1958, 1970:1-60). In general terms, the family is a primary unit of jural rights and liabilities. The family head is responsible for defending its interests against encroachment and for representing its members should they be involved in litigation with the members of other families. When a family member is found guilty of a wrongful act, fines are usually paid out of family resources. Also owing to Iban notions that personal character is inherited, a family's reputation suffers from the misdeeds of its past members.

title: Culture summary: Copper Inuit
text: While they do not state so explicitly, the Copper Inuit appear to prefer marrying people classed as cousins of varying degrees of closeness. Getting married was quite informal, with the couple merely setting up a separate domicile. Most marriages were arranged while the potential spouses were still children. Because of the shortage of women, due to female infanticide, there was often a considerable gap in age between bride and groom. In such cases a young man might live in the household of a prospective father-in-law for a period of several years while waiting for a girl to reach puberty, working in a form of premarital bride-service. At other times, gifts of important objects like sleds could be used as bride purchase. Before the birth of children, young couples often separated in a casual fashion with the woman simply transferring her household articles. On the other hand, given the usual shortage of women, marriage was sometimes broken through wife stealing, a practice which often led to homicide and the likelihood of a blood feud. Tensions created by this demographic imbalance resulted in short-lived polygynous marriages, with polyandry even more rarely practiced.

title: Social structures of the High Atlas
text: One appreciates this paradox of atmosphere, if one may venture to say it, which inspires in the humble montagnard jurist the poetry of the camel driver. The respect given by apparently barbarous cantons to the /326/ scholar, zaouia sheik or “cadi” is significant. 1 Can we go further than these observations? Does the antiquity of this procedural dualism permit evoking, across the gulf of time and distance, the division of the Roman procedure into two phases? We are far from the idea of finding again in the Atlas something that would recall the profound originality of the formula . But perhaps in the referrals to episcopal arbitration, frequent after Constantine, we can find something exciting for the imagination, if not serious for comparison. The first hypothesis has already been set forth by G. Surdon, /326 cont./ Esquisses de droit coutumier berbère marocain /Outlines of Moroccan Berber customary law/, 1928, p. 185, n. 1. One finds in this work very exact, but incomplete and scattered notations. For example, on the alwâh' , pp. 12, 142, 179, 181; on the instinct for patrimonial preservation among the Imazighen, pp. 35 sq.: on the true character of the rahn , pp. 196 sq.; the asghurt , p. 128. We are obliged to point out these coincidences with our own observations. And it is no less so that such a judge, often far from the place of litigation, cut off from any possibility of investigation, and chosen even because of that no doubt, does not base his decision on objective data at all, indeed sometimes not even on hearing the two parties. The decision is often presented in fact in the form of a letter delivered to one of the litigants, and undoubtedly solely on the evidence of his statement. One might be surprised by the fact that a rural society entrusts its most precious interests to such a whimsical magistery. But, on the one hand, the great majority of the conflicts are under the jurisdiction of prelaw and hence never come to procedural argument. And, on the other hand, the latter brings into play the not negligible factors of auctoritas . First, the weight of the person, of the writing, and of the reference to the Law. Then, the recourse to an external culture and ethic, felt as such, but to which one adheres at the appointed time and place, no more, and which one has intervene when it is necessary and when one wishes. In the second phase of this procedural splitting is read one of the attitudes of Chleuh /Shluh/ comportment with respect to Arabism and external civilization in general. We shall not engage here in a discussion of social psychology, which could lead far.

text: The procedure was for a suspected person to be brought into the centre of a ring composed of a council of chiefs, when the professor of Yalovaki seated himself on the mat opposite “the defendant,” and solemnly said to him, “Did you in very truth do this thing or not? If you lie concerning the matter, so will your soul be captured this day.” He then took a filmy scarf of finest tappa , and, immediately the answer was given, he twirled it over the man's head, as the Polynesians throw a cast-net, and if the man had lied, his soul was believed to be snared within it. Which belief, if the man really had lied, so weighed on his mind that he often went mad. Now comes the modern equivalent of the practice. The missionaries rightly stopped the Yalovaki , so the people felt bound to provide some sort of substitute. They saw in the earliest law courts the foreign method of “kissing the book,” which caught their fancy immensely; so to this day when there is an undetected crime, but especially when a man falls ill and declares that he must have been vakadraudrau'd , a secret meeting of the people is held, and all are more or less compelled to go through the Yalovaki practice, only Regui Vola (“smelling the Bible”--Polynesians do not kiss with their lips, they sniff with their nostrils) is used. This compulsory ordeal is not, of course, a thing to be approved of, and is not allowed, though only last year the Roko (native governor) of the Lau Islands wanted my permission to use it to detect witchcraft!

text: Kanuri descent is bilateral with an agnatic emphasis. Ego is a member of both his father’s and mother’s descent groups. Since this rule applies in turn to his parents, ego is consanguineously related to four grandparents. Bilateral kinship is referred to as dur (consanguinity) and is divided into dur bube or blood relatives (related to ego through his father), and dur chambe or milk relatives (related to ego through his mother). Inheritance follows Islamic prescription in that males obtain two parts to every one given to a female descendant. In terms of eventual material gain, this means that ego is allied to the patrilineal group to a greater degree than to any of his mother’s kin. Ego is also considered to be part of a patrilineally related group of males in terms of his legal responsibilities to the community. For example, in the case of the payment of compensation for manslaughter it is the patrilineal group which pays the fine, not just the individual.

title: Culture summary: Amhara
text: Social control is traditionally maintained, and conflict situations are resolved, in accordance with the power hierarchy. Judges interpret laws subjectively and make no sharp distinction between civil and criminal procedures. In addition to written Abyssinian and church laws, there are unwritten codes, such as the payment of blood money to the kin of a murder victim. An aggrieved person could appeal to a higher authority by lying prostrate in his path and shouting "ABYET" (hear me). Contracts did not have to be written, provided there were reliable witnesses. To obtain a loan or a job, a personal guarantor (WAS) is necessary, and the WAS can also act as bondsman to keep an accused out of jail. The custom now to be noted appears to bear the stamp of a later date, when the fears of supernatural sanctions were in some cases giving way to more mundane and materialistic considerations. In such a case, however, the Chief's representative might be empowered to say Kata m'ani (“Cover over my eyes”). The party who had sworn this “oath” might then, if he wished the matter ignored, pay the sum of £2 7 s. od. to the representative of the Chief. title: The herders of Cyrenaica: ecology, economy and kinship among the Bedouin of Eastern Libya
text: Officially, the descent and watan system disappeared overnight, but the actual process of change was much more complex. Particularly in remote areas, direct government intervention in the form of development projects or police activity was rare prior to 1972, and even when they did take action, officials often could not dictate the letter of the law. Working through local men of recognized authority, they attempted instead to mediate settlements acceptable to all the disputing parties, settlements which often involved the payment of blood money between groups of kinsmen and the staging of a SalaHiyya, a traditional Bedouin ceremony of reconciliation. In such cases the possibility of criminal proceedings and jail was invoked only as a threat, a move which lent to government mediation the force of binding arbitration. In the sphere of property relationships, every land holder still owned precisely the property he had acquired in terms of the watan system, but now he owned this property for a new set of reasons. Therefore, in terms of actual patterns of property ownership, the watan system remained intact, and many Bedouin continued to refer to this system as a means of calculating property relationships. On the other hand, some Bedouin appreciated the utility of the government system of land ownership as a means of enlarging or solidifying their property holdings, and these individuals have been among the most vocal and effective advocates of the government-sponsored theory of eminent domain. In this way innovative Bedouin have served as agents of primary importance in the implementation of social change in rural Cyrenaica. The following personal and case histories indicate the conditions which limited and motivated these Bedouin entrepreneurs. For the sake of clarity and coherence, I have included in this discussion only material on goat-herding Bedouin in the juniper forest (see Map 18 ).
