text: The 1913 roll commission had been effectively hamstrung by judicial wrangling over a definition of the term “mixed-blood”; such a determination was necessary before it could begin its work in earnest. Exactly how much white blood made an Indian a mixed-blood? Equity suits filed thus far had assumed that mixed-bloods possessed one-half or more white blood. Lawyers submitted three cases to test the principle. Judge Page Morris of the U.S. District Court ruled that a mixed-blood had at least one-eighth fraction of white blood. The U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals then overruled the decision, defining a “mixed-blood” as an Indian with any amount of “white blood,” no matter how small. Finally, on 8 June 1914, the Supreme Court upheld the decision of the Circuit Court of Appeals. Both Sayyid Said and his son Barghash corresponded with the sultans of Geledi and tried to woo them with gifts; and when the latter proved to be unpredictable allies, the sultans of Zanzibar sought to draw up commercial agreements with Geledi’s traditional inland rivals, the Biimaal. 78 . Pantano, La citta di Merca, pp. 9-10; Barile, Colonizzazione fascista, pp. 90-95. However, the Zanzibaris lacked first-hand knowledge of and real influence over politics in the Somali interior. Unable to penetrate the Benaadir hinterland, they had to be content with a nominal presence in the major coastal towns. There they found greater receptivity to their commercial ambitions and secured the right to build a garesa (fort) in Marka (in the 1860s), and later in Muqdisho and Baraawe, ostensibly to protect foreign traders. The Benaadir coastal families, always vulnerable to economic sanctions from the hinterland Somali, came increasingly to rely on the power of Zanzibar. It was the approval of town elders that enabled the sultans of Zanzibar to maintain fortified garrisons along the Somali coast through the 1870s and 1880s. 79 . text: In the old days, when there was little trade and the opportunity to obtain articles from foreign traders was still rare, debts arose through fines which one had shouldered but had not paid immediately; or owing to the fact that one had bought a buffalo or a pig from another village, because one needed a sacrificial animal for a meal for the dead or tribal feast at a time when one did not have any. Usually quite some time passed before one thought of paying and then only after the creditor had repeatedly pressed for payment ( mesingara ). If one could not pay off the debt all at once, then an amount was given to satisfy the creditor for the time being. This is called bakoe ntandje , “provisions of good faith”; sometimes also balara ntjaki , “rein of the debt,” because through this the creditor has the rein in hand to pull along the buffaloes still missing. Sometimes a pledge ( pangimpoa ) was given for a debt incurred. Sometimes years went by, so that the debtor died in the meantime. One then came to press for payment from his children. Sometimes they were dunned for a debt that the deceased had already paid during his lifetime. When a Toradja lies on his deathbed, he enumerates all the debts that he has outstanding. Now and then the dying person warns his children: “I leave no debts. If someone comes to dun you, do not believe him; he is lying. Then put a piece of pinang nut for me on my coffin; if the coffin moves, then stand up to him.” Such a pronouncement is called awili . If the children are dunned for debts that their father has not named, then the request is turned down with the words: “Our father did not speak to us of this debt and did not mention it on his deathbed.” If the other persisted in his demands and made it appear as though he would push it through by force, then an ordeal had to decide. text: In another case of Simaljore, the brother of Singrai Murmu was married as a ghar jawae in Dhamna. Singrai was in love with his sister-in-law’s younger sister, Gondo, but the girl’s mother was objecting to their marriage. Singrai went to Dhamna on the morning of the Baha festival. That evening the girls were throwing water on the boys but because Singrai was of another village, they did not throw any at him. Then on the spur of the moment, Singrai picked up some mud and rubbed it on Gondo’s head. Two of the villagers pounced on him, saying, ‘Why have you done it on her head? Why did you not do it on her body?’ Then they gave him a thrashing and took him to the headman. Next morning Singrai was sent to his own village and the matter was reported to his headman. A day was fixed for a joint meeting and early in the afternoon, the villagers of Dhamna went to Simaljore with axes, arrows and drums. When the headman said, ‘Why have you come?’, they replied, ‘A leopard of your village has scratched one of our calves.’ After that, they all sat round and Singrai was asked, ‘Did you do it?’ He answered, ‘I picked up a little mud and put it on her head.’ This was held to be iputut’ and two goats were then killed. Singrai was told to settle the marriage accounts, give the headman five rupees ‘for saving his head’ and pay a fine of five rupees ‘for doing it by force’. Then the villagers went back and Singrai gave a goat in Dhamna ‘to clean the ace’. A date was settled for a formal wedding and a matchmaker was appointed. The matter, however, did not end there for a little later Gondo’s mother changed her mind. The wedding, in her view, meant a second marriage in the same family and she believed that as a result one of the two girls would shortly die. So, in spite of the occurrence, she at last said, ‘I will not give her’. She did not press for payment and the matter dropped. Some time later, Gondo was married in Jobalda as a divorcee and there was neither a public wedding nor any smearing of her head with vermilion.

The girl's position in the family is a weaker one, and as a result she must pay a higher price for her intransigence. Most parents cannot afford to alienate one of their sons permanently, but there is no point in retaining the loyalty of an adopted daughter if she refuses to play the role for which she was adopted. Parents are therefore ready to apply whatever pressures are necessary in order to make the girl acquiesce to their plans. As a result, when it is the girl who takes the lead in opposing the marriage she must often go to extreme lengths to overcome her parents' determination. One village girl ran away to her natal home rather than marry her foster brother, and we know of at least three cases in which s[unknown] im-pûà left their foster homes to become prostitutes. They were either unwilling or unable to return to their natal families, and this was the only way in which they could manage to support themselves independently.

Thievery is usually an expression of disrupted social relations more than anything else, because it is difficult to conceal the fact that one has stolen something. Nevertheless, Tukanoans are becoming familiar with the idea of stealing and “getting away with it,” and they talk about earlier times when one’s cargo was safe in a canoe overnight, which is not always the case at present. A quasihuman or subhuman character is frequently imputed to cases of theft. Makú are said to steal, for example. When a danger exists of theft of cargo left overnight in canoes, the thieves are spoken of in somewhat supernatural terms - they are sometimes said to be able to fly, for example. The same is true for whites, who comprise another not-quite-human category. The Bará described to me a kind of forest demon who comes to a longhouse when everyone is gone and steals valuable objects, including any small children who have stayed behind. They must be given hospitality, they must not be involved in controversy of any kind, and they are confined to villages overnight while the cattle are at home. A ritual delegation is selected for a purpose. On one occasion this might be to prepare for a festival, perhaps soliciting cattle for the Prophet. text: North American tribal legal systems pertaining to property were an abiding focus of the Lipses' studies. Wild rice culture illustrated several theories distinguishing hunting-and-gathering societies from harvesting societies. Among hunters and gatherers, Julius Lips saw boundary lines clearly defined and rigorously defended. To trespass on the property of another meant certain death. With harvesters, however, boundary restrictions were lifted under certain conditions — the wild rice harvest was one. The rice fields belonged to all, and since the crop was of dominant importance to the economy, the law found its most important expression in a territorial principle that denied personal property rights to the cropland — in this case, areas of water where rice grew. 28 28. The ohemma plays an important backup role in credit extended between colleagues, which is often necessary to keep goods moving. text: Iyorkôsu’s text about Utishayem, PB’s notes taken in conversation with Iyorkôsu about the text, are in square brackets. Utishayem came to her lineage to have them take down the akombodam for her. When people had met, Anyam caught a chicken for the ishel of the woman. [ ishel kwase [h h m m] [unknown] ishel is a word connected with repairing women. Iyorkôsu says it has nothing to do either with ‘increasing’ or with ‘weak.’ He knows no other context for it. This is also done on the chigh and the igbe . Iyorkôsu knows no other on which it is done.] Somebody went to the bush to get locust bean and hul leaves. Nôr told them to bring a small pot full of water, with flour sprinkled in it; when this was done, Nôr took the twings of anune and hul and put them on each side of the pot. Then they brought a gourd dipper and a goat’s skull [The goat’s head, because it should be an actual goat. When you give money instead, you bring the goat’s head to count as part of the ceremonial. Even Iharev would do this, if they hadn’t a goat.] and the cassava stems--this is for the bag of salt. [The cassava stems are a substitute for salt of a kind which used to be made by the Udam near Ogoja, which Tiv used for this purpose. The fese were bags about a foot long, the thickness of the thumb, which this salt was put into. The bags were made of kughugh; the Udam made these little bags. Iyorkôsu says before European salt came, you bought these bags three for a penny. This is a tindi of the akombo, and would be shared among those who had the akombo, who would take it home and give it to their wives.] Then Fiase took down two of the salt and said it was a nanny goat [This akombo needs a goat to be repaired properly. But if no goat forthcoming, you give salt on it--in this case, no salt, so a further substitution is made (This makes two goats).], took out three and said it was the Asaa akombo [Asaa akombo . This is the total payment and includes agbar akombo, tens and twenties, etc. It means “that which is lost” in the akombo .], and took out a fourth and said it was the “sacredness of touching it.” [You gave money “because sacredness had struck it.” Sacredness ( chia ) is something which will not hurt you if you do not “know something on it” but will seize you if you do “know something”--that is, have guilty knowledge. If you “touch” the akombodam, then that is sacredness; if you do not, it isn’t. If you repair the akombodam, you remove ( dugh ) the sacredness--that is, if you touch the akombodam you strike ( ta ) sacredness. And when it is repaired, it is the repairman who “strikes sacredness” ( ta chia ) on it.] So Fiase asked Utishayem, “Where did you ‘touch’ the akombodam?” Utishayem said that once, when her husband wasn’t well, she had gone for wood, and she broke it off. [Implied here, says Iyorkôsu, is the idea that she took wood from a fallen tree on which she knew the akombodam had been erected to keep people from doing just that, but she did not respect ( chia ) it. Often a woman may not respect an akombo when it is erected--sometimes the akombo will seize her; sometimes not.] Then, another day, a plank ( kpande ) of the akombodam had been put into the indigo-hole, but she didn’t know it. She took some sliced yam and put it on the roof of the indigo hole to dry. She heard something fall with a little plop and when she looked under, she saw the kpande of the akombodam . That is how she ‘touched’ it. So Fiase told her to bring a “fine” ( wua tia ) and Utishayem gave a penny and a shilling’s worth of afese salt. When they had finished, Nôr began to dip out the beer; [This was dipped out and poured on the ground. If it had been real beer, they would have called out the names of the various elders and let them drink it, but nobody can drink this stuff, so it is poured on the ground. This has nothing whatever to do with the jijingi u ter --the latter is on the ifan, but not on the akombodam .] when he had finished that he took up the chicken and the goat[‘s skull] and began to ‘repair things’ with it. They took some cotton twine and tied it around Utishayem’s wrist so that when she leaves she can take it off and tie it on the wrist of her other child, who didn’t come to this. When this was finished, Nôr made the icegher and the ishel kwase is finished. Taking down the akombodam . [The akombodam is worst from the neck up--the analogy is helping somebody get the load off his head, which is to “shir” him.] When it comes time for the taking down, Nôr says he should be given a billy goat, a dog and an egg. When they have given them to him, Nôr begins to ‘repair matters.’ Nôr tells Utishayem to come bring salt. Ibi gives 1/-in salt. Ibi pays 3d instead of a billy goat and 2d instead of a dog. [ Nambe means to pay an acceptable amount in money or something else instead of the object actually required. If the mbatsav want to repair something and need a man but haven’t got him, they nyambe a nambe sha inyar (pay the difference in money).] Then Fiase tells Anyam to bring the chickens for taking down the akombodam . So Anyam goes and catches three chickens, and brings them together with a hindquarter of an antelope. [This quarter of antelope was in place of 2 chickens; he also gave 1/- in lieu of another chicken, making 6 in all.] Nôr takes hold of Utishayem and puts her into the “ akombo enclosure.” When Nôr had repaired everything, he takes the plank of the akombodam from his bag, and puts it on the ground. Then he cuts the throats of all the chickens. When he has finished, Nôr made a mark and sprinkled ashes to shut off an enclosure [If you talk to somebody outside this circle while you are in it, you must pay 2/-. This is called the ayom akombo, and is something like an atselegh --not quite a tindi is what this “cleverness of the akombo ” seems to mean. Ayomakombo include such things as the wuhe kura ’ing in the hindan ]--he also shut it off with camwood. Then Nôr caught hold of Utishayem and put her into the middle, and repaired everything, ending up with an ichegher [this ichegher is part of the mud] on the neck. When they had finished doing this in the compound, they got the things together and went down into the stream, and also repaired it down there. When it was repaired and people were coming back, nobody turned and looked back. When they got back from the stream, Nôr sprinkled water all about the compound of Akusa so that it would cool the bodies of everyone there. When this was completely finished, Fiase told Ibi to bring £1 for the “ten” and the salt ( agbar ); Ibi gave 15/-. Then Anyam got up and gave the tiame [Iyorkôsu never heard this word before; he wrote down what they said and figures it may be related to the wua tia . What he actually gave was ld.] and they made the ritual movements (chia) ( chia means “to make ritual movements” and is not to be confused with ta chia, which is a noun meaning “sacredness”], of “repairing things” on the various chickens and separately on the turtle. [Turtles may be eaten simply as meat--this is not an especial case. Iyorkôsu says it is very expensive, so people seldom eat the stuff.] When they had finished, the women brought out porridge for them to eat and make the ritual movements. Then they brought out a smouldering brand. Nôr soaked some vambe [leaves] in water, and everyone who had eaten had water smeared lightly on his neck. [This is peculiar to the akombodam, because if you don’t do it, the large sore in the throat associated with the akombodam will attack you.] When this was finished, Nôr said they should come pour flour in the cup from which the water was poured. Then Utishayem caught Nôr by the hand [while he lifted the plank]. The meaning of this was that she “picked up” (tô) the akombo . [Utishayem herself still couldn’t touch (in the English sense) the akombo directly, because she’s a woman. She picked it up through Nôr, however.] When you put a person inside this enclosure, the man who repairs the akombodam grasps the dog [This is the first Iyorkôsu ever heard of a dog having anything to do with the akombodam; dogs in other contexts, however, are “people.” The mbatsav sometimes kill a dog instead of somebody (or u genegh) and if a person gives you dog-meat, it is human meat and can become a flesh debt.], the goat and the chicken and he chants (ta chia) [ ta chia means to utter a spell or a chant--another form of “casting sacredness”], “This is my taking down of the akombodam today completely, and this is my washing you of the akombodam today completely, it is finished today.” When he has finished, he takes the chick, prepares the earth and makes (ta) the ichegh and falls to repairing things and making the ritual motions (ta chia) for “evil descend, goodness arise.” When he has finished, he kills the chick and throws it away. The matter of the marriage ward . When they had finished repairing this matter, Fiase asked Anyôgô, “Did Ngôngi eat Utishayem as his own ward? or did they say she was the ward of someone else?” Anyôgô said he hadn’t been there, so he didn’t know. Fiase then said, “Akusa, we’ll give you this girl today?” Then Uta called Utishayem and when she got there, Uta caught Utishayem by the hand and gave her to Nôr. As Uta did this, Fiase said that Uta hadn’t done the correct thing. So Uta told Akusa to bring a vingir gourd and they would “release” the girl and do it all correctly. Akusa went and got a vingir gourd and brought it, and Nôr said to give it to him, and also some sword grass. Nôr then called Utishayem and Uta prepared water to gber ifan, and Nôr released her properly. After they had all gber ifan, Utishayem put her foot on the gourd. Nôr took sword grass and passed it around her foot and cut it off. Nôr did the same to Utishayem’s child. When they had finished all that, Nôr took the girl [by the hand] and gave her to Akusa.

The action taken depends on what her husband has said, her reputation among the other men or even Shoort's feelings and mood. Shoort begins to demolish a hut with great caution, as if he were afraid of it. First he touches one of the hides which partially covers the hut or tent, then slowly grasps it and finally jerks it forcefully off the wooden frame and throws it to the ground, continuing until only the posts remain. I remember the Ariki Taumako standing outside his house Korofau one morning, looking ruefully at his sweet potatoes, which had been raided (probably by children living nearby), and realizing that there was little he could do about it. He made no public objection. The conventional reaction to discovery of a theft of one's property is the forua --the highpitched yell of protest. As time went on, this yelling was discouraged by the executive officials--on the grounds that as nearly everyone seemed to have been stealing it was mere [unknown]hypocrisy to yell about one's own losses; ‘with one's mouth full of someone else's food, maybe!’ But with chiefs the reason was different; they tended to refrain lest it be thought that they were anxious to maintain themselves at everyone else's expense; they were asharned to protest when all others were also suffering. Pa Ngarumea said in general terms, ‘the territories of the chief stand without interference only so long as the land is in good condition. But let things develop like this, they are thieved from. When the land is firm (food is plentiful) people pay respect to the things of the chiefs, but when there's a famine people go and make sport of them.’

title: 'I am very sorry I cannot kill you any more': war and peace among the Kapauku
text: Kapauku Papuans of the Western Highlands of New Guinea are organized into patrilineages, several of which combine into political confederacies. Within a confederacy law and order prevail, administered by a hierarchy of headmen called tonowi . Outside of these units political negotiations or wars characterized relationships. Thus war often began because a man had been injured by an individual of another confederacy. His wife might have been raped or induced to leave with her new lover. His relative might have died of sorcery, a pig might have been stolen or an economic contract broken. To receive support from the rest of his lineage and confederacy, the aggrieved man pleaded his case to the tonowi and demanded justice. If his case was regarded as justified, the tonowi of his lineage, of the allied lineages, and of the confederacy supported him and called upon their followers to go to war. If, however, the injured man started the war on his own, thus forcing his confederacy into a conflict without acceptable ethical reason and against the will of the tonowi, he risked capital punishment to be passed upon him in a secret sentence of the tonowi . Among the executioners would be included some of his closest patri-parallel relatives, such as his brother, paternal nephew, or cousin. They would kill the man with arrows shot from an ambush, not revealing their identity to the public. In such a case the war would be ended shortly.

text: During the Japanese occupation of Taiwan, registration of marriages, adoptions, divorces, births, and deaths was required by law. While failure to register would not affect the validity of a marriage, it would subject one to administrative punishment. Since the household register was under the control of the police, who were quite strict, registration generally took place. The requirement of registration was not an innovation on the part of the Japanese colonial government in Taiwan, but rather a refinement and continuation of practices that had existed during the Ch'ing dynasty. 22 See K. Hsiao, Rural China: Imperial Control in the Nineteenth Century 573 (1960). See also the requirements of registration under the section Hu-lu (household regulation) in the Ch'ing Code. Registration during Ch'ing times was, except for a brief period, to be that of the entire household including females. It was connected with the pao-chia (self-police units) system which required plaques on the outer gate of homes listing the members of the household. The system of registration was inefficient and was aimed particularly at control for purposes of taxation and corvée duties, thus focusing on adult males. The system was continued by the Nationalist government in Taiwan at the end of World War II and was reinstituted by the Communists in mainland China. While registration does not seem to have been a condition to entering a valid marriage either in Ch'ing times or under Japanese, Nationalist, or Communist law, 23 See M. Meijer, Specific Problems of Translation: Family Law, unpublished manuscript presented at conference on Chinese Communist Law, Bermuda, May 27-30, 1967, regarding the question of registration in mainland China. failure to register was penalized. text: The staff of the Korean Government-General (including affiliated offices) was at first composed of fifteen thousand persons, but by 1916 it had increased to 42,312 (of whom 4,146 were “maintained through other funds”). Of this number 23,483 were Japanese, with Koreans occupying only minor positions. Gendarmes and police were more numerous than all the teachers, physicians, priests, geomancers, and sorcerers taken together. They had not only the right to enter any residence at any time and to take part in court procedures; to serve as prosecutors in district courts, and to arrest without warrant; but also the right to pass “summary judgment” on those arrested. The punishment which policemen applied in such cases was usually flogging—thirty strokes. Out of eight thousand or more cases handled directly by the police each year, only thirty to fifty persons were able “to prove their innocence,” about one thousand were “pardoned,” and the rest were either fined or flogged. Flogging was never used to punish Japanese nationals, but only Koreans, because it was allegedly an old Korean custom. Political prisoners were invariably flogged. This has occurred on the levels of the tsu and even, to some degree, the family. In conflict within the tsu or village, as well as beyond the village, the tsu organizations through their leaders have always played a role in settling all conflict by mediation. While the several Hsin Hsing tsu have never been powerful organizations backed by extremely wealthy members and wealth in corporate land usually necessary to give them extensive local sociopolitical influence, tsu authority has recently been further weakened, as we have seen above, by the extension of the villagers' socioeconomic interests beyond the home area. As a result, even the tsu have apparently lost much of their ability to exert sanctions against their own members or their opponents. Thus, as a result of the weakening of the social hierarchy, there has developed a more general inability to use the former traditional respect for particular leaders of the landlord class or tsu as a force with which to settle disagreements.

The man replies: “I did no evil”. The prophet shouts at him: “Moi je le sais!” (But I know it!) Then, turning to me, he says: “Dieu m'a envoyé…voil j'ai attrapé lui…” (God has sent me—look, I've caught this fellow). As the man still makes excuses, the prophet says: “Let him confess straight away”, and later: “What is all this nonsense of ‘he says’ and ‘it seems as if’?” The chief secretary, an especially repulsive fellow, says cynically: “Nous sommes à vous, monsieur” (we wait for your confession, Sir). At last the man's inner resistance against the hostile mob and the prophet, whom he believed to be a real prophet, breaks down. Grudgingly he acknowledges himself to be a wizard. “After all”, he might have thought, “you can be a witch without knowing it”. (The public opinion is, however, that all those who want to excuse themselves in this way are liars). When he confesses the crowd hoots and mocks, and the young men have to restore order. The accused makes a last feeble effort to remonstrate, but the prophet just says: “let him be quiet—he has killed fifteen men”, and fines him. The man is led away. After this case, the proceedings are interrupted, and a telegram from a notable politician is read: “Accra. To XX…at XX…(date)…Have no objection to prophet ZZ carrying on with his work within the law. Stop. Have asked B…A…proceed today to E…with instruction. Stop. Greetings to prophet. Best wishes. NN (signature)”. People applaud the telegram, not realizing that this politician would violently oppose the “prophet” if he knew what was going on—things that were not at all “within the law”. In the meantime, the number of bands has increased to three, all playing frantically. Case 2.—A neurotic old woman is brought forward. Her face is distorted with hysteria and she balances on one foot. It seems as if the music of the bands gives her great pain. “Mamy, the prophet says that you are a witch”. She can scarcely hear, and answers “ehhhh?” A second woman is summoned and made to stand beside her. Behind the scenes, a gun is fired suddenly. The poor old wretch gets a shock, holds her ears in terror, her lips trembling visibly. A second shot frightens her still more. Attendants of the prophet explain to me that she was a witch who had wanted to kill the woman now standing beside her, but since the prophet had intervened, she could not do so and had become half paralysed as a punishment. The prophet would leave her in this state for a month. She was fined three pounds. At this juncture a spokesman from the chief protests that henceforth each witch should be made to pay a fine of twenty pounds for each murder laid at her door. Case 3.—An old woman. The prophet says: “elle a vraiment un diable”. (She really has a devil—witch spirit). She is accused of having killed one of her grandsons. Another grandson is called forward and made to stand beside her. He is a big fellow, quite a contrast to his shrivelled grandmtoher. The prophet says she has bewitched him causing him to become a drunkard and spendthrift. The prophet gives her a month to cure him of his drunkenness. She is fined seven pounds. Case 4.—A polygamist and his two wives. I understand that the accusation is that one of these felt neglected and therefore wanted to revenge herself by causing her co-wife to suffer from bloody flux. She achieved her aim and her rival was divorced. The woman is given a time limit of a month to repair the damage, and to restore normal periods to her rival, otherwise she will have to be brought to the prophet's village for treatment. Each time a case is settled, the music plays, people dance and shots are fired off into the air. Sometimes two or three bands all play different pieces of music at the same time! The prophet now leaves the scene and further cases are tried by his secretary. Case 5.—An old woman is accused of killing a number of people. She speaks for a long time, but in vain. “Do you know MM? and NN? and XX? Where are they? Are they dead? Yes, they are dead—you have killed them!” She is fined fifteen pounds. Case 6.—A stout man in the prime of life. The secretary says: “Dis-lui il a tué contre son argent”. (Tell him that he has committed spiritual murder in order to make his fortune). With his money he was said to have built a house. At first the man seems very sure of himself and laughs at the accusation—but under the pressure of the crowd's hostile atmosphere he becomes quiet and no longer remonstrates. Case 7.—Again a middle aged man is accused of committing spiritual murder and confesses. Case 8.—Cannot be tried today, since the defendant is away at A. People are dispatched to fetch him. Case 9.—Three sisters, priestesses or mediums of one of the smaller sects. One of them is accused of having turned her sisters into “fetish priests”. All three are accused of having committed incest with their own brother. One of them protests strongly, and is, therefore, charged ten pounds. The other two get away with three pounds each. They are told to fetch their “fetish things”, and bring a wooden cross (round which they had tied strips of white calico) and their calabash-rattles. Case 10.—An old woman is accused of having stolen her daughter's womb. She promises to return the womb to her daughter in a month's time and is fined seven pounds. Case 11.—A long case between a man and his wife. The woman is charged with having deprived her own son of his livelihood. She is charged ten pounds and the E. chief will have to settle the palavers between the man and his wife. Case 12.—A middle aged man. When charged with the murder of two persons, he confesses and is fined six pounds. He is almost dumbfounded and walks away a broken man. Case 13.—A nervous driver with flickering eyelids and a constant stutter, is accused of having poisoned a fellow driver's mind until he became disturbed in his head and went mad. No denial of the allegation is of any avail. He is charged to bring the other driver back to his senses and is fined six pounds. Case 14.—A middle aged, medium sized stranger. Accused of first making the local people mad and then effecting their cure if payment is offered. “You killed a lot of people in this town”. A fine is duly exacted. Case 15.—This case is deferred, since defendant is absent. Case 16.—Two of the young men of the prophet's “police force”. They are accused of pilfering and admit the charge. The crowd laughs heartily. They are charged one pound each. “If I were to charge them more, they would only steal the money to pay the fine”. This is considered a capital joke and the day's proceedings end in general merriment.

Kimudwe (alias Dulnuan) of Tupplak is a famous, or rather an infamous, sorcerer. Owing to a quarrel with one of his nephews, Butlong, over a debt, he performed an ayak to cause the latter’s death. Butlong was informed of the fact by one who, eavesdropping below Kimudwe’s house, heard the prayers and incantations. On a certain day on which there was a feast in Ambabag, to which Kimudwe was nearly certain to come, Butlong waylaid him, f[illegible]ng a rifle at him from cover near Ambabag. His marksmanship was atrocious. Before he could reload women rushed out from the village and covered Kimudwe with their bodies, interceding, and stating that there was not sufficient certainty that Kimudwe was guilty to justify his nephew in killing him. (Thi occurred in the interval between Spanish and American rule.) Kimudwe is reputed to have killed by means of sorcery several of his kinsmen. Recently a child died in Tupplak whose death was attributed to him. He killed, it is said, the son of Bahni, another of his nephews. Bahni sent Dulinayan of Ambabag as a go-between to Kimudwe to challenge him to an ordeal, saying that he had no intention of killing him, even if guilty, owing to the peculiar prejudice of the Americans against such doings, but for his own satisfaction he wanted to know if Kimudwe were the sorcerer. He stated that in case Kimudwe won in the ordeal, he (Bahni) would pay a fine of a gold bead for having accused him falsely. This was an unusually large fine. Kimudwe refused, or rather evaded, saying: “If I am a sorcerer, it is a case of the entire family, including Bahni, being guilty.” In other words, he took refuge behind the Ifugao doctrine of collective responsibility (see sec. 4).

title: Structure and authority in a Bedouin tribe: the 'Aishabit of the Western Desert of Egypt
text: Among the Bedouins, the conceptualization of an authority structure in the role of ’aqila relates to the high value which they place upon a peaceful and orderly world. Children in al-Qasr are taught that one of their serious duties in life is to mediate conflicts, especially, when they are potentially situations which may lead to protracted conflict. And, in a segmentary society where a member’s status links him to many different groups in differing degrees of importance, all quarrels are potential group wars. The Bedouin child knows that his elders, and God, want him to follow “the path of the good” ( tariiq al-khair ). Mainly, this involves helping others to follow “the path of the good” by “bringing them back together” when they are in conflict. When two individuals quarrel and refuse to return to “the path of the good,” this brings ’aib (“shame”) to each of the persons. When two individuals quarrel, setting off a group conflict, this brings ’ar (“shame”) to the respective corporate groups of the individuals (Abou-Zeid 1966). Against individuals who persist in the ways which cause ’aib to himself, or ’ar to his group, certain sanctions of both a secular and sacred nature may be imposed: expulsion from the group and the curse of God are ultimate coercive interventions in the process of conflict regulation.

title: Klamath ethnography
text: A marriage payment is a social obligation. It is not a negotiated transaction as with the Yurok, Hupa, and Karok, for example, where indeed the social status of the family is measured in exact accord to the sum paid for the bride. Here failure to pay, which can be only a confession of inability, leads only to a lowering in social esteem. It is consonant with this that the bride is in no sense a chattel; she may leave her husband at will, and she certainly cannot be disposed of as a possession. Bride purchase is as inapplicable a term as can be found for the Klamath practice. In the interchange of presents which follows marriage the advantage lies most frequently with the husband’s family. Payment constitutes an obligation, a seal of respectability. This is the well-nigh universal situation in North America if payments enter at all; it is a far cry from the commercial, contractual bride purchase of Africa, for example. The peculiarity of the Klamath is that failure to pay constitutes a social stigma. This is clearly explicable as a function of their geographic position, lying between the tribes to the west, with their clear-cut monetary evaluations of social relations, and the tribes of the Great Basin to the east, utterly devoid of any such sentiments.

text: The tertiary group in Bedouin society is by definition the blood-vengence group. However, in view of the common values and pragmatic interests of its members, the secondary group fulfills this function. Traditionally, when revenge killings were carried out according to the lex talionis , it was usually at the hand of some member of the victim’s tertiary group. In the case of protracted conflict, such as extended feuds or war, secondary groups, and even whole tribes, became involved. If the tertiary group is in the structural sense a blood-revenge group, the ’aqila is the corporate sole of the blood-revenge corporation: an important function of the ’aqila’s office derives from this. The ’aqila is responsible for the collection and distribution of the blood-money. It is this specific authoritative function of the office which is the necessary condition for the existence of a corporate group. If there is no ’aqila to collect blood-money, then a kinship segment is not a corporation and it will merge into another group headed by an ’aqila in order to realize collective benefits.

I asked why no one had ever stopped her and called a Band Constable. The answer, when I finally found a constable who would tell me, was that this woman's elderly mother practised “bad medicine”. People in the community were too frightened of her power to induce physical illness (frequently in forms symptomatically similar to Bell's Palsy) to risk antagonizing her. text: Traders in illegal goods relied very heavily on advance information on raids and policy changes for survival. Even a few hours' or minutes' warning might be essential to enable them to pack up their stalls or at least run away from a police raid. Neighbors and fellow traders cooperated fully in passing on news of the immediate movements of police or soldiers and on the identity of informers. Larger-scale traders also cultivated contacts with officials or soldiers for information farther in advance, which could prevent losses or even allow occasional windfall profits. Advance notice of when and where goods would be sold at controlled prices was as effective and less risky, for example, than receiving diverted supplies and deserved the same reward. During the strict enforcement periods of 1979, this might be only a warning not to come to the market tomorrow, which saved the trader an arrest or a beating. Rumors that some moneychangers had used advance notice of the currency exchange to unload their notes on unsuspecting colleagues provoked great bitterness, since the amount of old notes individual traders had on hand varied so widely with their state of credit and repayment. Sometimes these private tips were confidential, in that traders could not pass them on too widely without endangering their informants. The same contacts might also provide protection after traders were caught, but this was more difficult to conceal.

title: Observations on Northern Blackfoot kinship
text: The age-authority hierarchy was further reinforced by economic considerations. It was the pattern to associate prestige with generosity. Those who gave generously increased their own prestige, providing that they did not bankrupt themselves thereby. Within the extended family it was the practice to encourage siblings to give to their juniors. This was not only an expression of endearment or of aiding a weaker person, as it was often phrased. It also had the effect of putting juniors in the debt of seniors. To be sure these debts were not the same within the family as outside the family between unrelated persons, for repayment between relatives was not categorical. Yet we have such instances as a young man raiding for horses to repay his father. The father had given horses in settlement to a husband whose wife had had an affair with the son. In other cases where an older brother had made his son a favored child, the younger brother gave abundantly to this favored child, “to repay the older brother for his kindness to him in his youth.” We have also noted that young men returning from war always gave some portion of their booty to older brothers. text: The Toradja insists very strongly on his rights, or, rather, he is most strongly set on being put in the right. If he believes that he is right, he feels himself secure in the protection of his ancestors and is calm about the outcome of the matter; if necessary, he will fight for it; in no case will he give up his claim. And even if he personally were inclined to do this, if the offender does not belong to his immediate kin group, then his own kin group feels itself wronged together with the offended one and will urge him to seek his rights. And not only the living kin-group, but also the deceased, thus the gods, are interested in the case, and if the offended one does not want to exert himself to let justice take its course, he himself is guilty before the ancestors, who have instituted the customary law and will therefore not permit it to be abridged. This comes out particularly when strangers unintentionally violate the customary law, whereby generally no one can be personally offended; for instance, by beating on a drum in the village temple or firing a shot in a harvested rice field before the harvest festival has yet been celebrated. In such a case people insist, with all politeness, but strongly, on the payment of the fine, but only to uphold the adat. Otherwise the ancestors would bring afflictions upon /195/ their descendants who are not faithful to their duty to maintain the customary law. We were never fined for a personal matter, although we or one of our people have indeed been in circumstances in which a Toradja would have been fined. But in connection with transgressions against the adat (always committed in ignorance, of course), we were never spared. In some cases they made an appeal to our compassion to pay the prescribed fine.

title: The kings of Buganda
text: This was how King Mutesa adopted Christianity. When he got the services of Dallington, he also called Masudi the Arab. The latter used to write in Arabic what Dallington read and translated from the Book of Moses. After the translation had been made, the king became a very devoted reader. The king had some special favourites among his pages such as Mponyebuwonyi and Kaganyulo. When they saw that the king had adopted Christianity, they refused to eat meat in the palace and went on grumbling: “The king is becoming an unbeliever. He has adopted the European religion.” When the king learnt that his pages had started calling him bad names, he became very very angry. Hence he arrested about seventy people who practised the Mohammedan religion and sent them to the Namugongo execution place where they were burnt to death. The story of these Muslim martyrs is not well told by Kaggwa and for a long time it escaped the attention of scholars. Recently, however, F. B. Welbourn and Katumba have written an interesting article about them. 26 This reference is to FBW’s and Katumba’s article, “Mutesa Buganda”, Uganda Journal, Vol. 1/1 (1934), pp. 22-49. Kaggwa’s account in fact gives the impression that these were executed because they abused the king for his Christianity. It would appear, however, that this was to have been the occasion for their execution rather than the cause. The evidence suggests that the Muslim pages were stricter upholders of Islam than Mutesa. 27 Gomotoka in Makula; R. D. Musoke in Ebifa of 1917. And their zeal resulted from the new inspiration provided by the Egyptian Sheiks who had been despatched with Linant by the Khedive. Kaggwa makes no reference to these Sheiks. H. Mukasa, however, does, and he states that they found fault with Mutesa’s religious practices. His mosque for example faced west instead of east and he himself was uncircumcized, despite the fact that he conducted the prayers in the royal mosque. Furthermore, his refusal to be circumcized, suggested that the meat served in the court was slaughtered by uncircumcized butchers. The Egyptian Sheiks condemned these practices, whereupon some of the pages refused not only to participate in the prayers conducted by the king, but also to eat meat at the Court. This was treason enough, but because the pages had no meat to eat, they resorted to methods which were little less than robbery. Hence there was a general outcry from the chiefs residing in the capital. It was a combination of these factors, therefore, which led to the execution of the Muslims. But even after that Mutesa remained a practising Muslim.

title: Alabi's world
text: In July 1777, the missionaries witnessed two spectacular public executions of Saramakas who had been convicted of witchcraft. 36 36. In 1773, the missionaries had merely alluded to the execution of another accused sorcerer, said to have killed nine people, who was burned at the stake (St 3, pt. 1, 184). And in 1776, Postholder Wurzler reported yet another witchcraft conviction: a “slave” named Angula was found to have killed a child in Chief Etja’s family, but Etja, instead of having him burned to death, wanted to turn him in to the whites for a bounty (Hof 94, 21 July 1776). Alabi, as village captain, presided at the decisive council meetings and participated fully in these events. 37 37. Throughout his lifetime, Alabi continued to believe fully and matter-of-factly in the reality of witchcraft-sorcery. In 1798, a missionary described how, on the 20th [February] a strange negro, with several women, came hither from the upper country [i.e., from upstream]. While we were conversing with them, Arabini came running, and with great authority, without ceremony, drove them away from us and out of the village. We were quite astonished, and knew not what to think of such conduct, as visitors are always well received. But he afterwards told us, that the above-mentioned negroe professed the art of mixing poison [sorcery], and boasted that he had already destroyed many people by it, so that he was everywhere to be shunned. ( PA 3:51) Because the Moravians considered such proceedings primarily political and juridical, rather than religious, they seem not to have been overly concerned that Alabi was playing a central role. For them, wísi meant “poison,” not “witchcraft” or “sorcery” (as it did to Saramakas). The Moravians seem to have thought that some Saramaka wisi accusations were well founded, while others were trumped up-as in any system of criminal justice. 38 38. From yet a third perspective, that of twentieth-century social anthropology, these accusations of wisi must be seen as part of a complex social process-unfortunately, too complex to analyze on the basis of the materials the missionaries provide. Modern studies of witchcraft among Suriname Maroons would suggest, however, that an understanding of the lengthy process from initial whispered accusations to public executions or lynchings (which continued into the 1950s in Djuka) would require a very close acquaintance with local village politics and personalities (van Wetering 1972, 1973). It is clear at least that eighteenth-century witchcraft helped “explain” unusual deaths (e.g., the death of three siblings in quick succession), permitted the collective release of strong emotion, and, through scapegoating, effected the elimination of certain marginal or “difficult” individuals (largely innocent and defenseless people who were often among the aged, the handicapped, those who had risen too far too fast, the patronless, and so on). In one unusual late eighteenth-century witchcraft craze, among non-Saramaka Maroons belonging to the group of Kwami, allied with Boni, twenty-eight villagers were quickly accused and executed in a Jim Jones-like frenzy (Hoogbergen 1985, 130).

text: The greatest of all human crimes, murder, was punished with death; but the act was open to condonation. Unless the family were appeased, the murderer, as with the ancient Greeks, was given up to their private vengeance. They could take his life whenever they found him, even after the lapse of years, without being held accountable. A present of white wampum, sent on the part of the murderer to the family of his victim, when accepted, forever obliterated and wiped out the memory of the transaction. (101) Immediately on the commission of a murder, the affair was taken up by the tribes to which the parties belonged, and strenuous efforts were made to effect a reconciliation, lest private retaliation should lead to disastrous consequences. If the criminal belonged to one of the first four tribes, and the deceased to one of the second four, these tribes assembled in separate councils, (57) to inquire into all the facts of the case. The question of the guilt or innocence of the accused was generally an easy matter to determine, when the consequences of guilt were open to condonation. The first council then ascertained whether the offender was willing to confess his crime, and to make atonement. If he was, the council immediately sent a belt of white wampum, in his name, to the other council, which contained a message to that effect. The latter then endeavored to pacify the family of the deceased, to quiet their excitement, and to induce them to accept the wampum in condonation. If this was not sent in due time, or the family resisted all persuasions to receive it, then their revenge was allowed to take its course. Had it chanced that both parties belonged to one of the four brother tribes, a council of this division alone would convene, to attempt an adjustment among themselves. If, however, the family continued implacable, the further interference of mutual friends was given over, leaving the question to be settled between the murderer and the kindred of his victim, according to the ancient usage. If the belt of wampum was received before the avenger had been appointed, and had left the lodge on his mission, it was usually accepted as a condonation, but if he had gone forth, the time for reparation had passed. The family then either took upon themselves jointly the obligation of taking what they deemed a just retribution, or appointed an avenger, who resolved never to rest until life had answered for life. In such cases, the murderer usually fled. As all quarrels were generally reconciled by the relatives of the parties, long-cherished animosities, and consequently homicides, were unfrequent in ancient times. The present of white wampum was not in the nature of a compensation for the life of the deceased, but of a regretful confession of the crime, with a petition for forgiveness. It was a peace-offering, the acceptance of which was pressed by mutual friends, and under such influences that a reconciliation was usually effected, except perhaps, in aggravated cases of premeditated murder.

This involved saying “ fääjiro ” as an expression of respect on meeting a chief. If further required that one crouch or crawl in the chief’s presence if he was seated, for it was forbidden to have one’s head on a higher plane than his. One avoided initiating social interaction with a chief, unless the need was urgent, in which case one made him a gift and then waited the chief’s pleasure. One could not persist in refusing a chief’s request without being guilty of namanam tekija (arrogant behavior), nor could one address him harshly or belligerently. For persons other than his relatives, a chief occupied the most heavily taboo status with respect to behavior of this kind. 15 15 The other categories of persons who shared this status with the chief were jiuag and pwëny (navigators). His consanguineal and affinal kinsmen, however, behaved toward him in accordance with the status positions which he occupied as their kinsman, at least as far as their being “taboo from above” him was concerned. Other formalities were also accorded a chief. When he walked along a path with a party of people, he went first, unless the path was difficult. In the latter event someone went ahead to clear the way. While crawling behavior and the expression “ fääjiro ” are no longer exhibited, a chief still walks first today and the people still feel themselves to be “taboo from above” him.

text: Vulnerability to a common set of kúnu s implies a number of specific social obligations. Bêè members have a strong vested interest in one another’s personal morality, in the prevention of acts that could lead to the creation of new kńu s. Moreover, whenever such an act is committed, bèê members have a real stake in effective collective action, such as reparations to the wronged party, if he is still alive. Common kúnu vulnerability stands behind the concept of the bêè as a “legal person,” the idea that one bêè member is responsible for the debts of another, that one may be beaten for the adultery of another, and so forth. The meticulous division of many classes of material goods into equal shares for distribution throughout the bêè rests squarely on kúnu belief. text: Gonzalez was made sargento major of the tekoá of Takuaratý. Marciano Iturbe was a delegate to the departmental government, and it was logical that Gonzalez be appointed, 77 . The rank of these Chiripá officers was sometimes dirigente, comisario, or teniente . Sargento was the term most often used in the 1950s and 1960s. Today they are more often known as comisario. complete with papers and a military uniform. Gonzalez acted at the behest of the deputy of the alcalde of Igatimí to bring Chiripá accused of thievery or other malfeasance to the local police station. After miscreants had been thoroughly beaten and forced to work in the alcalde’s garden, Gonzalez would escort them back to Itanaramí, assuring the leaders that they would create no further disturbance. 78 . Chiripá express strong ambivalence toward systems of justice meted out by a frontier alcalde. Without a judicial system, the alcalde or comisario decided guilt and determined the sentence. Accusations defined blame, especially if leveled by a mestizo. As with poor mestizos, confessions were then extracted by beating the accused with a bludgeon or short whip, called a tatú ragúe (“armadillo’s tail”). Punishment was generally performed as unpaid labor for a local bureaucrat or military officer, and sentences could stretch to weeks or months of work for serious violations, such as murder. Despite the injustice and brutality, many Chiripá fear the contemporary legal system even more than their ancestors did that of the frontier. Today, the accused can languish in dark cells for months before appearing before a judge, who will inevitably find them guilty. Then, rather than being forced to labor outside, they are sentenced to years in windowless rooms behind bars in the capital city. Sargentos’ rights were strictly limited to the indigenous community. They were not, however, full military personnel; they received no salary and were not allowed veterans’ rights to special land purchases or pensions. Their only compensation was the doubtful prestige the position afforded them in their own communities and access to a few benefits from the local military officials—a military uniform and a free meal when visiting the post.

It has no precedence in that State either before or after the passing of the Native Jurisdiction Ordinances of 1883 (as amended 1910), nor does any custom admit it. In our custom there is a fixed amount of money payable for seducing another man's wife, i.e. depriving a person of his wife to make her one's lawful wife. If, for instance, Kwaku, whose fixed ayefare fee is £4 16 s. , had his wife seduced by Kwadjo, the amount of damages that Kwaku has to claim is £8 16 s. , a double of the principal amount of ayefare. (The 16 s. which is called Nteho or Nterakyire “sanction fee”—and which is an appendage to £4 as much as 1 s. is an appendage to a guinea—is not doubled.) The fine payable to the Paramount Chief for seducing another man's wife—whether the case was taken to Tribunal or not—is £12, i.e. twice as much as for violation of an ordinary oath. It is patent, therefore, that the consawment dowry or head-money and the expenses, need not be paid by the seducer. These are repayable by the wife's parents to the husband now divorcing his wife on account of the seduction, but the parents may have to reclaim the head-money, but not the expenses, from the seducer before the validation of the marriage. We may add here by way of parenthesis that if the wife's family choose to let the new husband pay the expenses, they may do so by adding it to the old head-money, thus making the wife's head-money heavier than before. But this practice is rarely followed.

title: Negroes in Brazil
text: A large number of popular terms have arisen which seem to designate the various racial combinations in the population. However, a) these terms are descriptive not so much of racial descent as (1) of the actual physical appearance of the individual in question, and (2) of his social rank; b) they may vary with the person employing them, and with the same person at different times and under different circumstances, and especially with the status of the individual being referred to and with the relation of the speaker to him. Caucasian physical traits possess prestige and also disproportionate aesthetic value among all social ranks and colors, 41 41 With the possible exception of a few colored intellectuals, particularly in São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro, who deliberately seek to valorize “negritude” (blackness), although their attitudes in this respect seem to be rather ambivalent. although the local “somatic norm-image,” in the phrase of Hoetink (1961), is considerably “darker” than that in the United States, as is borne out, for instance, in attitudes toward the morena (see pp. 136-38). The rise in rank of colored persons, a) occurs primarily by reason of demonstrated personal or occupational competence, educational achievement, the accumulation of financial resources, or fortuituous circumstance; b) is sometimes aided by brancos who are linked by parental, godparent or other bonds of sentiment to the individual in question (cf. pp. 353 ff.); and c) is accomplished by individuals as individuals, so that conflict on the basis of either color or class is relatively subdued (cf. Thales de Azevedo 1955a:195). In their attempts to rise in rank, persons of color are handicapped by the fact that color has long been identified in Brazil with a slave condition and hence became, long ago, a criterion of rank. This is the role of dark color logically to be expected, given the history of slavery in Brazil and the Americas, where slaves for centuries were blacks taken from Africa by Europeans and their descendants, who possessed a more advanced technology, to labor on their plantations and in their placer mines. However, had this “historic accident” been of reverse character, that is, had Africa at the time of the discovery and early exploitation of the Americas itself possessed technological superiority, and had Africans and their descendants then discovered America and taken to work on their plantations European slaves from a Europe of less advanced technological development, dark color—and not white—would today, in all likelihood, carry prestige. Being white would then probably be a decided disadvantage, a definite handicap, since long ago white color would have become a criterion of inferior rank; and whites would then want to be black and to have children blacker than themselves. However, the restraining influence of color in Brazil today, a) varies inversely with its intensity (as do all the other criteria of rank); b) is not the determining criterion, as in South Africa or the United States, but only one of a series of conditioning circumstances, similar (as far as most persons are concerned) to those with reference to age, sex, lack of personal competence, lack of skills, lack of financial resources, or lack of education; c) varies with the individual and with circumstance; d) may change permanently during an individual’s lifetime; e) may be less significant than some observers have thought; and f) may be tending to decrease, as more individuals demonstrate their ability to overbalance the restraining influence of color by the accumulation of other criteria of rank (provided, of course, that changes now under way in the economic and sociological structures do not alter this trend). Although cases of discrimination involving colored persons undoubtedly occur, they are not necessarily due exclusively to color. In any given case, the circumstances are complex and need further study. If the discrimination turns out to be due only (or largely) to color, it will in most cases be because color is one of the criteria of rank. However, nowhere in Brazil is it supported by public opinion. On the contrary, it receives severe and widespread condemnation, in press and elsewhere, and legislators hasten to pass laws bringing it under repressive legal sanction. In other words, public opinion and public action invariably are in favor of —never against—the darker portion of the population. Nevertheless, in any conflict situation, the lack of one of the determinants of status—namely, light color— just as any other lack, may be seized upon, to a person’s disadvantage, by competitors. Numerous common sayings regarding Africans and their descendants (cf. pp. 362-65 of this book) which originated during the slave epoch, and which long ago lost all, or most, of their function as stereotypes (cf. Florestan Fernandes 1959:328), occasionally are employed by brancos but ordinarily with a smile and in a humorous manner and when colored persons are not present. Moreover, actual behavior tends to belie these common sayings; and they are even used in jocular fashion by colored persons themselves. Nevertheless, they are remnants of a superordinate-subordinate relationship in a former caste order and, as such, constitute threats to status in possible conflict situations, and also potential aids to the development of group-consciousness. To these hypotheses, there might be added the following one, suggested by Wagley (1963b:154): “The ability of ‘people of color’ to improve their status...varies considerably from community to community according to the possibilities open to them.” Wagley’s further statement that “rural Brazilian society has a rigid class structure” would seem to be valid for all Brazil outside pioneer areas. We might consider also in this connection the observations of Hutchinson (1963:45-46) at Vila Recôncavo to the effect that “the population is becoming...class-conscious” and that “there is an increasing desire to rise in the social hierarchy”; as well as the discovery by Harris (1963:79) of a degree of tension in the large middle group at Minas Velhas; and certain data turned up in the studies in central and southern Brazil. These (and other) considerations raise the following additional hypothesis: Both social mobility and class-consciousness are increasing; and this increase may be heightening color-consciousness, particularly in the intermediate ranks, by reason of the comparative rigidity of class lines, and the fact that color is a criterion of rank.

Thus, in certain circumstances, when blood money is accepted after a homicide, by the victim’s group, the offender’s group may be required to pay an additional small annual fee, known as sana’ . If this condition is accepted it means, in effect, that the offender’s group is insufficiently strong to maintain its free status and is faced with the possibility of relegation to client status. 19 19 In one case I recorded of sana’ payments, the paying group was, when I worked among its members, wealthy in animals and numerous in membership. The demand for sana’ was aggressively made and the alternative, of feud, was made clear. Many of the offender’s group wanted to withhold payment, but the shaikh thought it prudent to pay a small amount on this occasion once more, because he was standing as a candidate in the parliamentary elections which were about to be held. This payment could only achieve a postponement of hostilities, for the obligation to pay sana’, once accepted, is a committal in perpetuity. Secondly, if hearsay evidence is accepted, powerful groups have been able to appropriate the lands of their weaker neighbours and coerce them into accepting client status. In one form of feuding, the offender’s group deny responsibility for a homicide. This is not only a challenge, but an implied rejection of the nobility of the victim’s group. The latter should avenge the death of a member and the insult added to the injury, but to achieve this double retribution, status may in fact be forfeited when the challenge is issued by a group powerful enough to overwhelm. Some groups have chosen a loss of pride rather than a surrender of status.

text: In 1958 the committee appointed for the examination of the possibility of applying the system to Awlad Ali noticed that villages in the sense of a compact settlement similar to that existing in the rural area simply do not exist in the Western Desert region. There are a few settled communities in the area but they are scattered homes or a few stores. These communities have no identifiable boundaries or administrative existence. The area as a whole is divided into ten administrative districts, each having a police station. These districts correspond to the old Senusia Zawyas which played an important role in maintaining order in the era until the First World War. Until that time the area was divided into fourteen zones each of which was under the jurisdiction of one of the zawyas. The zawyas were mainly religious centers, or shrines, inhabited and directed by a member of the Senusi order of Cyrenaica. The role of the head of the zawya was to teach the Qoraan and spread the teachings of the Senusi order. One of the ways the zawyas attracted followers was through distribution of food and clothing to those who joined it. The zawyas also provided places of refuge for those who needed protection since no one could force his way into the sacred zawyas. Because of their religious position which put Because of their religious position which put them outside the tribal structure, the leaders of the zawyas played a significant role in mediation and settling disputes between various tribal segments. text: Anything owned by an individual is thought of by the Iban as an extention of his person. As a result, any loss or damage done to an individual's property also harms its owner, not in a direct physical sense, but spiritually, by causing injury to the owner's spiritual personality, or soul ( samengat ). In the same way, a physical injury, or the loss of social esteem is like wise thought to harm an individual's soul. Thus any act that causes another person bodily injury, loss of social respect, or does damage to his property is seen by the Iban, not only as a secular grievance, but also as an attack upon the victim's soul, and in all such instances ritual compensation is required to repair the spiritual injury done, in addition to any secular damages, or indemnities, that might be claimed. The notion of the soul thus has a highly important legal dimension in Iban adat and secular forms of redress are reinforced in cases of personal loss caused by others by ritual reparation.

text: In 1858, Lemreway was once again made available to crofters, most of whom came from the fishing townships where population pressure was building up. After the disastrous potato famine of 1846-7, and the final failure of the kelp industry from 1840 to 1844, the population of the Outer Isles experienced great hardship. By the early 1850's, the lotting of the crofts and the rapid development of the fishing industry brought a period of prosperity and the population grew rapidly especially in the fishing townships of the Minch coast. The prosperity was such that numerous cottars built houses on the lotted crofts, and their stock-keeping on the common was tolerated because of the demand for fishing crews. About 1884, the system whereby each boat was tied to individual fish merchants, who advanced meal and provisions against the catch, was discontinued. When this system was replaced by the auctioning of catches, such was the privation in Lewis that the Royal Commission investigating the poverty of the population in 1888 found conditions almost as severe as those prevailing during the potato famine forty years earlier. It was during this period that the Park Deer Raid occurred: Park became a Deer Forest in 1883 at the end of the grazier's lease. In 1888, as a demonstration of their grievances, a large number of crofters from the Park townships went into the Deer Forest and killed about 200 deer, cooking the meat in the open for all to see. Some were arrested but after trial acquitted. 3 Stornoway Gazette, 27.1.59. text: The term baum , or aum , describes any meeting convened by a local leader. These meetings may be held for a number of reasons. In the Saribas, for example, a general distinction is made between baum mit and baum besai , “small baum ” and “large baum ”. The latter is typically a conference of headman and other leaders from neighbouring communities who gather to discuss some matter of general concern. The baum mit , on the other hand, is convened by the longhouse headman, usually for the purpose of resolving a private matter between his followers. The matters dealt with are frequently disputes, or complaints brought by one longhouse member against another. Here the Tuai Rumah acts, not so much as a judge, as an arbiter, attempting sometimes with the help of kin and neighbours, to persuade the two parties to settle their differences amicably. Such baum usually make an informal settlement possible without the need for judgment ( dibechara ); otherwise, except in the case of serious wrong-doing, they represent the first stage in the process of adjudication and provide the Tuai Rumah with an opportunity to gain a better understanding of the issues involved in the dispute.

text: SINCE THE COLONIAL PERIOD [unknown] Under British rule murder and certain other defined offenses, as well as cases involving non-Africans, were placed under the jurisdiction of Protectorate Government courts. Ganda courts have tried offenses against uncodified “native law and custom,” such as theft, assault, or insolence to a chief, as well as all kinds of civil wrongs not reserved to government courts; and they have also tried offenses defined by laws of the Buganda or national governments, such as adultery, arson, tax default, offenses against agricultural regulations, or drunkenness. Chiefs acting as judges had the assistance of a few subordinate chiefs chosen in rotation, and interventions by the general lukiiko have been gradually discouraged. The necessity of producing a written record, however summary, of the cases heard has tended to make the procedure more formal, and such technicalities as the inadmissibility of evidence may be raised. But professional lawyers cannot be employed in Ganda courts, and the chiefs themselves have little or no special judicial training; hence decisions were more usually determined by substantive justice than by legal technicalities. There was right of appeal from the subcounty to the county court, and from there to the principal court at Mmengo; decisions were subject to the revision of the judicial adviser, an officer of the Protectorate Government. Punishment was and is by fine or imprisonment. With the introduction of magistrates (see page 114), who receive some special training, procedures have become still more formal, and there is now only one level of court below that of Mmengo.

text: A belief in witches is to this day, and always has been, one of the most deeply- seated notions in the minds of the Iroquois. The popular belief on this subject rose to the most extravagant degree of the marvellous and the supernatural. Any person, whether old or young, male or female, might become possessed of an evil spirit, and be transformed into a witch. A person thus possessed could assume, at pleasure, the form of any animal, bird or reptile, and having executed his nefarious purpose, could resume his original form, or, if necessary to escape pursuit, could transmute himself into an inanimate object. They were endued with the power of doing evil, and were wholly bent upon deeds of wickedness. When one became a witch, he ceased to be himself. According to the current belief, he was not only willing to take the life of his nearest friend, but such an one was the preferred object of his vengeance. The means of death employed was an unseen poison. Such was the universal terror of witches, that their lives were forfeited by the laws of the Iroquois. Any one who discovered the act, might not only destroy the witch, but could take to himself the dangerous power of deciding who it was. To this day, it is next to impossible, by any process of reasoning, to divest the mind of a Seneca of his deep-seated belief in witches. 1 But a year since a woman was shot on the Allegany (Seneca) reservation, on the pretense of witchcraft. Such instances have been frequent among the Senecas within the last fifty years. Not the least singular feature of the case is that they sometimes confess the act. There may be some foundation for this strange delusion in the phenomena of nature.

If his body was not hale, then he could not serve efficiently as a representative of his people and a medium for his gods. This was exemplified by an Ariki Kafika, Pepe, about nine generations ago, according to tradition. 3 See We, The Tikopia, Genealogy I, p. 397. History and Traditions in Tikopia. He was said to have been afficted with severe yaws (framboesia), and therefore to have abdicated in favour of his younger brother, Tuisifo. In comment on this story, one of the senior men of rank in Kafika said, “If a chief dwells and contracts yaws, then he is put on one side to the rear. He is taken to the rear since he has become bad. Even while the yaws is slight he goes to the rear, because it is an evil thing. When the yaws stands in (the body of) a chief, it is the doing of the gods. It is bad, therefore is set to one side that another chief that is good may be taken.” The underlying reason for this setting of a chief aside in Tikopia belief was not that the disease itself was physically contaminating or ritually destructive, but that it was a manifestation of the displeasure of the gods towards the chief. There was a suspicion that he had done something wrong. In any case, his power with the gods must have been ineffective, otherwise he would not be suffering. Yet such a general principle was not necessarily carried out in practice. The Ariki Fangarere in 1929, an elderly man, had been afflicted with a debilitating tropical ulcer in his foot for a number of years, but he still carried on his duties as chief, and I heard no suggestion that he ought to retire. He himself had not expressed any wish to abdicate. This may have been due to the fact that he was extremely active in economic and ritual affairs despite his lameness. Occasionally a concession was made to him as when, during the rites of the Work of the Gods, he came by canoe over the lake instead of walking round the shore with his co-chiefs. As I saw in 1952, such a concession could also be made to a chief on account of the weakness of old age. The affliction of the Ariki Fangarere was treated, then, rather as weakness than as fault. Yet that weakness of old age of the Ariki Kafika was regarded as deleterious to the welfare and prosperity of the land was borne out by opinions in 1952. 4 Reymond Firth. “Some Principles of Social Organization,” Journal Royal Anthropological Institute, Vol. LXXXV, 1955. pp. 9-10.

You rejoice it with four chickens and give an agbar payment of five shillings.” [3] “The disease the megh gives people: it ruins your body. If the megh seizes you, your luck (ikôr) also is ruined. If you copulate with a menstrous woman, the megh will seize you and your luck will be ruined.” The megh has to do with adultery, especially adultery with the wife of another member of the ward-sharing group. Once such adultery has occurred, you have to counter it by “ tsura ’ing the woman megh .” This is the ritual with the jôndu gourd described above. A case of it is to be found in Justice and Judgment among the Tiv, Moot No. 1, pp. 169-171; another in the case of Utishayem, above. After adultery of a woman, the next person to copulate with her (whether it be her husband or some other man) will sombu if this is not done--the word means “break” as of a bone or “quake” as with palsy. The danger here is especially great, Iyorkôsu says, when a man is getting into middle age and his adult sons begin to sleep with his wives before he grants them the privilege of doing so. In this case, the father is likely to sombu if he is not told and the megh repaired for the wives, and the sons. When we asked, Iyorkôsu claimed he never heard of a case in which a man had slept with his son’s wife--it was always the son sleeping with the father’s wife. He told us that father-daughter incest was a great foolishness (bumegh), but did not require repairing. In case of brother-sister incest, the girl becomes the marriage ward of the man and is removed from the protection of the rest of the ward-sharing group. It is a very great shame (dzege kunya), and you must pay “fines” (tia) to your agnates both in the daytime and at night (that is, it gives the mbatsav of your lineage an excuse to demand a sacrifice from you--and eventually, of course, you must give yourself).
